utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, the Defence of Slobodan Praljak raised a number of errors of law and fact committed by the Trial Chamber. The Defence admits that all its grounds of appeal are well founded. We shall today only address certain grounds of appeal and emphasise some of the cardinal errors that eviscerate the entire judgement and that invalidate Slobodan Praljak's conviction. From the outset, we wish to emphasise that nothing has been -- nothing has been properly established in the judgement. The judgement is inchoate, confused, contradictory, and unintelligible. It is based on rumours and assumptions, which in turn are based on a selective and approximate selection of the evidence that has often been assessed out of context and mischaracterised. In breach of Article 23.2 of the Statute of the Tribunal, the Trial Chamber has omitted to provide reasoned opinions on its essential findings. The judgement ignores the basic standards of international criminal law and general principles of law, i.e., the presumption of innocence, the standards of proof beyond all reasonable doubt, and it seems to ignore that the burden of proof lies with the Prosecution. When the Trial Chamber establish a state of occupation, i.e., our second ground of appeal, paragraphs 42 to 56 of our brief; and an international conflict, i.e., first ground of appeal, paragraphs 7 to 41 of our brief, it committed a series of errors of law and fact that led to erroneous findings regarding, inter alia, the role played by Croatia, but first and foremost the role played by Slobodan Praljak, errors that invalidate all Slobodan Praljak's convictions based on Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I [Microphone not activated] but please slow down as much as you can, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal is to be applied, namely, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, the Trial Chamber must establish the existence of an international conflict or of a state of occupation. A state of occupation can only follow from an international conflict or an invasion. In the present case, there was no invasion. Therefore, to establish a state of occupation, an international conflict must be established. But also a cessation followed by the establishment of power -- by the establishment of authority by the foreign power that then replaces the authorities that were in place before the occupation. No foreign power has established its authority over the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Trial Chamber did not reach that conclusion either. The Trial Chamber concluded in paragraphs 579, 580, 583 to 585, 587, and 588 of the judgement, volume 3, that the HVO had occupied certain territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina - the HVO, namely, the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is quite impossible. The HVO cannot occupy the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The HVO had been created by the Croats who lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was a body that had been recognised by the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. See 3D647 and P1988. It was also one of the components of the armed forces, 3D647, P339, and P1988. How could they occupy a territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina? This is from legal and logical standpoint quite impossible. A people that lives in a location cannot occupy such a location. It cannot occupy the land of its forefathers. It cannot live on a territory where it has been living for centuries. This is quite impossible. The absurdity of the conclusions of the Trial Chamber is reflected in the Prozor municipality, which - according to the conclusions of the Trial Chamber - was occupied by the HVO. Paragraph 578 of volume 3 of the judgement. In Prozor, during the elections of 1990, the Croatian Democratic Party won an absolute majority, 1D920, transcript page 3478. No change-over of power occurred during the purported occupation, and the authorities that had been legally elected continued to exercise their authority. There was no foreign power. The local authorities that had been legally elected continued to exercise their power, and the Trial Chamber found that there had been an occupation. The Trial Chamber committed a series of errors of fact when it concluded that there was a state of occupation, but it established no legal element required for such an occupation. By concluding that the HVO had occupied certain territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Trial Chamber committed an error of law of such a magnitude that any discussion on the state of occupation is quite simply impossible. Nowadays, international law affords protection to civilians and to their property in internal conflicts - fortunately - and in international conflicts. International Judges do not need to conjure up an international conflict or a state of occupation to try international crimes. Suffice it for them to apply the appropriate standard. If Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal cannot be applied outside an international armed conflict or a state of occupation, the other articles that essentially cover the same type of conduct require no international armed conflict, neither -- neither an international armed conflict nor a state of occupation. However, in this case, no matter what the nature of the conflict is, no matter what article needs to be applied, no rule of law has been applied correctly, and this does not warrant the conviction of Slobodan Praljak, for he has not committed the crimes he is charged with. As in the state of occupation -- in a state of occupation, the Trial Chamber committed an error when it considered that the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina was an international conflict. The evidence on the record do not lead to the conclusion that the Croatian army participated directly in the fighting. I shall not repeat the arguments we have set forth in our appeal. I will, however, emphasise that an international witness stated that the ECMM had no tangible indications of the presence of the units of the Croatian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Transcript pages 20486 to 20487, 20501 and 20504. The presence of the Croatian army units was assumed; but despite all the efforts deployed to establish it, the latter was never confirmed. Transcript page 20504. And I'd like to specify that this is testimony of an international witness. The individual members of the Croatian army went to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some of them joined the HVO, others joined the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Transcript pages 40076 to 40077. These people retained their administrative ties to the Croatian army but had been incorporated either in the chain of command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the chain of command of the HVO. The Trial Chamber established this in volume 1, paragraph 775. Some members -- some of them -- some members of the Croatian army were also members of the HVO and of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Slobodan Praljak himself was a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. 3D3510. Not having really established the direct presence of the units of the Croatian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Chamber held that the Croatian army exercised overall control over the units of the HVO. Judgement, volume 3, paragraph 35 -- 545 to 567. If the Trial Chamber had properly applied the standard established by the case law of this Tribunal, namely, the standard of overall control, it should have then assessed all the elements of control assessed in there altogether and determined whether -- on this basis, whether the requisite degree of control existed. Appeal judgement, Aleksovski, paragraph 145. In the Tadic case, the Judges held that the requisite degree of control of a state could be considered proven when a state played a role in the organisation, the co-ordination, the planning of military actions of a military group, in addition to funding, training, equipping, and providing operational support to it. Paragraph 137 of the Tadic appeal judgement. In this case, the Trial Chamber did not establish that Croatia had played a role in the organisation, co-ordination, or planning. All that it established is some vague assistance which, moreover, was provided, both to the HVO and to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is -- can be found in the transcript pages 9878, 40076, 40077, and a multitude of documents we have cited in our appeal brief, paragraph 18, 19, 22, 23, and 24. The Republic of Croatia provided weapons to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Republic of Croatia trained the members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Republic of Croatia had three logistical centres of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that operated freely on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. The Republic of Croatia tended to the wounded of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What state? What state would have provided the weapons, the equipment, the training, and the logistics to the enemy army -- or the hostile army? The answer is, quite simply: No state would do such a thing. In addition, the Trial Chamber totally overlooked the particularly unglamorous situation in which Croatia found itself during the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Republic of Croatia did not take part in this conflict. It was solicited by the international community as a whole and by some individual states asking it to calm down the situation, organise negotiations, and provide a solution. The findings of the Trial Chamber concerning the visit of Minister Gojko Susak at the time, Minister of Defence of Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina, volume 3, paragraph 552, perfectly illustrate the misunderstanding of the Trial Chamber of the situation. At the time, ministers of defence of a number of countries visited Bosnia-Herzegovina. The visit of the minister of Croatia carries no more weight or is not more important and is no different from the visits of other ministers of other countries that took place without interruption. This visit is part of the role imposed by the international community on Croatia and does not demonstrate in any way that Croatia took part in the conflict; quite the contrary, it was to provide a solution and put an end to it. No doubt, there was no international conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993 and the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims was an internal conflict, between two people that were living in the same state for centuries. I would, however, like to return to the standard of overall control which the Tribunal has applied ever since it worked on establishing an international conflict. The Tribunal admitted that the overall control standard is less stringent than the standard affirmed by the ICJ and explained that this approach allowed for a better protection of civilian victims. Appeal judgement Aleksovski, paragraph 146. If the purpose of international human law standards is to protect civilians, the purpose of Judges must be no other than to apply the standards. It is not incumbent upon the Judges, and particularly not in a criminal case, to interpret the standards in a broad or loose way with the sole aim of convicting the accused. The Judges must apply the law. And the rules of criminal law, those that may lead to the conviction of an individual even in an international context, must be strictly interpreted. Despite the fact that I have already mentioned, namely, that Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal is not the sole article applicable to the alleged facts in the indictment and that the Statute provides for other articles that may make it possible to enter a conviction for alleged facts if they are proven. The approach adopted by the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case is today challenged by the ICJ. It attaches the greatest importance to factual findings and legal qualifications set forth by the ICTY to rule on the criminal responsibility of the accused. The ICJ held that the ICTY is not required to rule on the issue of international responsibility of states. Appeal judgement of the ICJ dated 26th of February, 2007, paragraph 403. To adjudicate indicate on the application of Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal, the Judges of the ICTY have no choice and must adjudicate indicate the nature of the conflict. When they adjudicate the nature of the conflicts, it would be fair and legally correct and wise to refer to international law that has been well established and that is not familiar with overall control but effective control. Indeed, when the Tribunal establishes an international conflict according to its own standards - which is a problem in itself - it engages the responsibility of the state which according to it would have participated in this conflict. For, from an objective standpoint, if the state had participated in the international conflict, then it - normally speaking - could be held responsible. However, if the Tribunal does not apply the rules of international law, its findings are worthless as regards responsibility of a state. They will be deemed not applicable to that state, and this situation may give the impression that the Tribunal is not applying the law. It is difficult to understand how an international jurisdiction applies one rule, whereas another one relating to the same legal issue - i.e., international conflict - would apply another rule. If the Tribunal applies a rule of law which is disavowed by the ICJ, this situation could have a snowball effect in an avalanche, in which the Tribunal in the end will lose all credibility. I will now address your question number 2 and will discuss the crimes committed in the municipality of Mostar. Regarding the question regarding the errors committed by the Chamber relating to the destruction of the Old Bridge, the Defence would like to emphasise that errors committed by the Trial Chamber when it analysed the destruction of the Old Bridge are not isolated but are part of a series of errors which led to erroneous findings. By concluding that a crime against humanity, persecution, and a crime of -- and a war crime, spreading terror in Mostar, the Trial Chamber considered the snipers, the bombings, the destruction of the Old Bridge, the destruction of mosques, the isolation of the population, and forced transfer. But none of these facts have been properly established with regards to Slobodan Praljak. The errors relating to the destruction of the Old Bridge are a perfect illustration of the errors committed by the Trial Chamber that established no relevant facts as regards persecution or spreading terror in accordance with a well-established criminal procedure and international criminal law. None of these facts can be attributed to Slobodan Praljak beyond all reasonable doubt. The errors in connection to the destruction of the Old Bridge are ground of appeal number 23, paragraph 280 to 296, have without doubt an impact on crime of persecution and spreading terror, for they show that these have been tried on the basis of erroneous facts and must therefore be reversed. The Trial Chamber committed an error of law when it held that the destruction of the Old Bridge was disproportionate. I will not cover this or this ground again. Paragraph 290 of 296. But it also committed an error of fact when it held that the HVO had destroyed the Old Bridge. I would like to now just give you one example. Once again, the Trial Chamber disregarded evidence which did not suit it. It decided that the -- the testimony of witness Vinko Maric was not credible simply because it contradicted the theory of the Chamber. It's written -- this is in the judgement, paragraph 1322. The Trial Chamber has broad discretionary powers when assessing the evidence, but it does not hold arbitrary powers and cannot substitute a theory which is not founded on the evidence to a witness's testimony. The same errors can be found in the findings of the Chamber as regards all the other crimes. The snipers, for instance, the Trial Chamber admitted that a number of -- volume 2, paragraph 1032, that a number of these crimes could not be attributed to the HVO. It also recognised on a number of occasions and for each incident identified that it was unable to establish the exact location of the origin of fire. This is also in the judgement, volume 2, paragraph 1077, 1087, 1107, 1130, 1134, 1147, 1150, 1151. In such a situation, how could the Trial Chamber - not knowing where -- what the origin of fire was - how could it in such a situation reach such a conclusion, namely, that the snipers belonged to or were under the control of the HVO? No reasonable trier of fact could have reached such a conclusion. The same applies to the bombings, the origin of which is confirmed by no document. P4573. This same situation applies to the mosques. The Trial Chamber established that eight mosques had been damaged or destroyed in 1992, well before any conflict erupted between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Trial Chamber also established that only two mosques were intact and still standing in January 1993, but nobody knows what happened after January 1993. Judgement, volume 2, paragraph 1369, 1370, and 1371. How in such a situation could the HVO be responsible for the destruction of ten mosques between June and December 1993 since at least eight, if not all ten mosques, had already been destroyed? If one follows the reasoning of the Trial Chamber, the HVO would have nothing else to do but to destroy the already destroyed mosques, of course. From a theoretical standpoint, one can complete the destruction of damaged mosques. But in that case, in that case, the Trial Chamber would have had to establish what kind of damage had been caused before that date and what damages had been inflicted by the HVO. It did not do this. It simply attributed - absent any evidence and in a totally arbitrary fashion - the destruction of the mosques to the HVO. The errors in connection with the Old Bridge are part of this same series of errors by which the Trial Chamber attributed, without any form of proof and in an arbitrary fashion, all these criminal acts to the HVO. The Defence recalls that a reasonable trier of fact should be reasonably convinced that the Prosecution has established all the essential facts of a crime beyond all reasonable doubt. If at the end of the trial the crime has not been established, the principle of in dubio pro reo must be applied. Appeal judgement Martic, paragraph 55. In this case, in this particular case, the Judges of the Trial Chamber did not apply this principle. Likewise, when the Judges established the presumptions based on indications, it is not enough to state that the evidence may lead to a reasonable entering -- to a reasonable finding of guilt. This finding cannot be the only finding possible. If another conclusion can -- or finding can be reasonably drawn from the evidence and when it does not exclude the innocence of the accused, he must be acquitted. Appeal judgement Celebici, paragraph 458. Once again in this case, the Judges of the Trial Chamber have disregarded this principle. Briefly, regarding your question number 8, the crime of spreading terror, the Defence submits that crime of spreading terror requires a specific intent directed at spreading terror, will establish a case law in the Galic case, appeal judgement, paragraph 104. This intention has not been established in this case. The Trial Chamber correctly stated that the crime of spreading terror requires that the main purpose of the act be the spreading of terror. Volume 1, paragraph 185 and 187 -- 195 and 197. However, it is not sufficient to enunciate the principle; it needs to be applied to the facts. But the Trial Chamber established that the activities of the HVO were directed at sectors where the military objectives were located. Judgement, volume 2, paragraphs 1003, 1009, 1013, and 1014. This finding alone, since the activities are directed at military objectives, are sufficient basis to exclude terror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. You haven't -- unless you tell me that you haven't finished, you haven't answered the second part of question 8, which is the --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is question 8?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What the impact would be if the Appeals Chamber found that the Trial Chamber failed to provide a reasoned opinion in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, our conclusion are the same regarding the second part. As far as we're concerned, the judgement in its entirety must be invalidated. And regarding the crime of spreading terror, it has not been established. But in addition, the Trial Chamber did not provide a reasoned opinion; and for us, that amounts to the same. This invalidates this conviction, this particular conviction, and has an impact, of course, on the other crimes in which spreading terror does play a part. May I resume, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, I would like to provide a response to question number 10. I believe that it is slightly similar to the question you asked. At this stage of the procedure what I would like to say is that -- and I would like to address this immediately afterwards. We consider that there is no joint criminal enterprise and no common purpose, so any question relating to JCE 3 is moot, notwithstanding this irrelevant of any standard which was applied or which should have been applied to the Trial Chamber relating to this issue. Of course, we are prepared to return to this issue, if necessary. We consider that the error committed by the Trial Chamber in this case relates -- is to be found in its findings on the common criminal purpose. The Trial Chamber held that the common -- the JCE was established mid-January 1993 to achieve its political objectives, volume 4, paragraph 44. Firstly, political objectives do not amount to a common criminal purpose. I take this opportunity to inform you that Slobodan Praljak's Defence agrees entirely with the arguments of the Defence of Jadranko Prlic and Bruno Stojic on all questions relating to the existence of a joint criminal enterprise and a common criminal plan. Having thus determined the political objective, the Trial Chamber held that according to the interpretation of the leaders of the HVO, this political plan included ethnic cleansing, paragraph 44, volume 4. Nobody knows who these leaders of the HVO were, who would have attributed a criminal dimension to a political plan. We don't really know which crimes were included in this plan. In this plan the term "ethnic cleansing" is not a legal term and is much too vague to specify the alleged crimes. The Trial Chamber has, therefore, never clearly established the crimes which were envisaged in the initial plan and cast doubt on those persons who may have had knowledge of this criminal plan. The common criminal purpose was purportedly expanded in June, volume 4, paragraph 57. The Trial Chamber did not establish with -- all the members of the JCE and Slobodan Praljak, inter alia, agreed to the common criminal purpose. It did not even establish whether they were informed of such an expansion. What crimes were included in this expanded enterprise? This time the Trial Chamber cited a multitude of crimes, paragraph 66, but in the following paragraphs, paragraph 67 of volume 4, the Trial Chamber held that the members of the JCE knew that most of the crimes -- most of these crimes were committed and intended to have these crimes committed. Most of these crimes. Which crimes are included in the term "most"? A judgement rendered by a criminal court must be specific which is not the case; it is not specific, unintelligible, confused, contradictory. For a member of a JCE to be held responsible for crime committed by another, this crime must be part of a common criminal purpose. Appeal judgement Brdjanin, paragraph 418. And to determine whether a crime is a part or is not part of a common criminal purpose, such a crime must be clearly established, which is not the case in this particular case. Beyond the fact that the initial common purpose or its supporting from a legal point of view were not properly established, the Trial Chamber made a factual mistake by ignoring the relevant facts. I'm talking here about the broadening or extension of the JCE. Even if the Trial Chamber established that in June 1993 the ABiH was attacking HVO positions, judgement, volume 2, paragraph 880; and volume 4, paragraph 57, it decided without any valid reason not to take this into account. If the Trial Chamber had taken into account the attack launched by the ABiH over HVO in June 1993, it should have held that the subsequent events were the consequence of this attack. In this case, the Trial Chamber would not have needed the imaginary common plan that created only on the basis of the Prosecution's allegations, but the Prosecution's allegations are no evidence and do not demonstrate facts. For the sake of clarity, I would like to add that the attacks of the ABiH do not warrant any crime committed in response to these attacks, but they shed another light on the situation and explain differently the events. These attacks cannot be ignored; they must be taken into account if one is to properly assess the facts. The Trial Chamber made findings but it instantly forgot them. The Trial Chamber's conclusions are particularly unclear but also contradictory with regard to Slobodan Praljak. Indeed, according to the Trial Chamber's findings, the common criminal purpose would have been enlarged in June 1993 with the siege of East Mostar and was mainly implemented in Mostar. Judgement, volume 4, paragraphs 57 and 59. And the same Trial Chamber held that there is no evidence about the role that Slobodan Praljak played in these events in Mostar before 24 July 1993, judgement, volume 4, paragraph 577. Hence, when and where Slobodan Praljak could have received the information about the enlargement of the common criminal purpose is still a mystery. So is the fact that Slobodan Praljak had or not adhered and joined this extended purpose or whether he contributed to it in any other way. And since this information is unknown, Slobodan Praljak can only be acquitted for the crimes that he would have committed through his participation to the JCE. We do not know either how the Trial Chamber reached the conclusion that leaders of the Republic of Croatia were part of the JCE. Once again, the findings of the Trial Chamber are contradictory. Indeed, the Trial Chamber held that President Tudjman supported the Bosnia-Herzegovina division by incorporating part of it in Croatia or, alternatively, with the establishment of an autonomous Croat entity within the BiH. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 10. The establishment of an autonomous Croat entity within BiH does not imply splitting it and directly contradicts the conclusion of the Trial Chamber that President Tudjman supported the Bosnia-Herzegovina division. Besides, dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina was not some invention of President Tudjman because he always opposed to this division. I'm referring here to P6454, page 2. Dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina was one option proposed by the international community. So once again, the international community raised this issue. P108, page 48. The Defence indicated in its appeal brief, Ground 5, paragraphs 70 to 88 -- so the Defence indicated that all the documents showing without any ambiguity that President Tudjman continuously advocated for internationally recognised borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina and against any separatist intention. President Tudjman's motives are not important. His personal opinions or beliefs are not important. What matters in criminal proceedings are actions an intentions, and both fully -- and both show that full support to independent sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina within the internationally recognised borders. When Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised, President Tudjman made everything he could to co-operate with Muslims. P134. Even if some international bodies kept on considering for their own interest dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina, 1D896, page 3, President Tudjman or Croatia never supported this option. Unfortunately, the majority of the Trial Chamber showed complete misunderstanding of the historical background in the Balkans, hence the wrong inferences regarding President Tudjman's statements about a Croatian Banovina. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 22. In order to fairly grasp what Tudjman meant, one has to know a little bit of history. Banovina was only an administrative region created in 1939 with the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in order to find a solution to the Croat question which was already raised at the time, and the Kingdom of Yugoslavia was made up of several Banovinas and the Croatian Banovina was only one of them. And when President Tudjman referred to Banovina, he does not refer to an independent state and sovereign state but to a whole territory; and actually, it does not even include all the territories, all the current territories, of Yugoslavia. There is it no Istria, no Baranja, nor Dalmatian Coast. So why, why would President Tudjman have wanted to recreate this Croatian Banovina? This is completely preposterous. The Trial Chamber also ignored the fact that until April 1992, Bosnia-Herzegovina was no independent and sovereign state in the sense of international law. Bosnia-Herzegovina was part of Yugoslavia, which was disintegrating. The discussions and talks that happened before Bosnia-Herzegovina claimed its independence have to be assessed within this context. In 1991 until April 1992, nobody knew whether it would become independent or not. The Trial Chamber assumed - wrongly and without any tangible evidence - that President Tudjman planned to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina; and afterwards, it assessed all the evidence in light of this erroneous presumption, which led it to ignore President Tudjman's statements or misconstrue their meaning. This approach of the Trial Chamber culminated with the erroneous and completely unreasonable conclusion that civil servants of the Republic of Croatia would have been involved in a JCE. Same for the Trial Chamber's conclusions that President Tudjman would have been the real leader of the Croat of Bosnia-Herzegovina delegation in January 1993. The evidence in this case merely show that Tudjman was in London. Transcript page 16673. And there's a gap, being present and participating. There is a gap between taking part in negotiations and leading a delegation. And those gaps, the Trial Chamber did not even try to fill those gaps. But beyond all this evidence, transformation, the very conclusions of the Trial Chamber are confused and contradictory. Indeed the Trial Chamber could never include the leaders of the Republic of Croatia within the common criminal purpose; they didn't even try to do it. It only claimed that the leaders of the Republic of Croatia, among others President Tudjman, supported the creation of an independent or autonomous Croat entity in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The leaders of the Republic of Croatia do not appear in the common criminal purpose; and in all paragraphs referring to this plan, the Trial Chamber only mentions HVO leaders - wrongly once again - but it only mentions them or Croat community leaders in Herceg-Bosna. In reviewing the common criminal plan, the Trial Chamber never mentioned Minister Susak or General Bobetko, who would have been members of the JCE. President Tudjman is only mentioned twice but in a context that puts him not within the JCE, but as the contact person of the international community - judgement, volume 4, paragraph 49 - or attending a meeting with President Izetbegovic, paragraph 52. This is not enough to infer that leaders of Republic of Croatia were part of a JCE. Besides the Trial Chamber excluded itself the leaders of the Republic of Croatia from the common criminal purpose when it held that the crimes were the result of a plan established by the leaders of the HZ HB. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 65. Croatian leaders simply disappeared. It also excluded them from ... from -- sorry. Strike this. It also excluded them of any criminal purpose when it held that leaders of HVO gave some criminal interpretation to the political plan envisaged by the leaders of the Croats in Bosnia and some leaders of the Republic of Croatia. These conclusions of the Trial Chamber confirm that the leaders of the Republic of Croatia could have pursued some political objectives, but these conclusions do not show any criminal intent or criminal objective and cannot place them within a JCE. Your Honours, with all due respect, you have -- this Tribunal has jurisdiction to ... you have jurisdiction to judge -- [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This Tribunal was given a mandate but it has no jurisdiction over political party, over the people, and even less over a sovereign state. The Trial Chamber is bound to establish some evidence in order to convict an accused on the basis of a JCE. One could accept that these strict criteria cannot be held against alleged members of the JCE who are not accused. Nevertheless, it would be problematic to involve through JCE people who cannot defend themselves, and this all the more problematic when those people held high-level political or military functions within an independent state. Their implication in a criminal enterprise could have extremely serious consequences because it could make a state liable. As a consequence, the Trial Chamber cannot be satisfied with a general statement without any tangible proof which actually contradicts other findings that it made. Similarly, the same mistakes -- or the Chamber erred with regard to Slobodan Praljak. The Trial Chamber held that Slobodan Praljak assisted and attended meetings with some leaders of the Republic of Croatia. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 522. But according to the Trial Chamber, Croatian leaders did not participate or were not involved in the establishment of the common criminal purpose. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 44. So these meetings cannot lead to the conclusion that Slobodan Praljak was involved in any way to the joint criminal enterprise. The Trial Chamber also tried to establish that Slobodan Praljak was implementing in Bosnia-Herzegovina a policy established by the Republic of Croatia. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 527. But the Trial Chamber could find no criminal element in the policy of Croatia. As a consequence, implementing such a policy - which in any way was not evidenced - does not demonstrate in any way that Slobodan Praljak participated in the common criminal purpose. Paragraph 525 of the fourth volume of the judgement is also completely incomprehensible. How could Slobodan Praljak have implemented in 1992 - 1992, Your Honours - the common plan that was only established in 1993? Actually, over the relevant period for Slobodan Praljak, between January and November 1993, the Trial Chamber could only establish that he attended two meetings. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 523. These meetings can in no way be linked to the common plan and cannot be used as evidence showing that Slobodan Praljak was participating in a JCE. The first of these meetings was held on 15 September 1992, and its objective was to convince the representatives of the Herceg-Bosna Croat community to endorse the agreement with the Muslims in order to find a peaceful solution. At this meeting, Praljak only explained the situation in the field and his intervention had the same purpose as the whole meeting: Finding a solution that would end fighting between Muslims and Serbs. P5080, pages 11 to 23. The objective of the second meeting was the same: Implementing agreement with the Muslims. P6454, page 3. And once again, in his intervention, Slobodan Praljak only described the situation in the field. Actually, and to put it simple, the whole case - as lengthy as it may be - has no evidence that Slobodan Praljak knew, one way or the other, that there was a common plan in January 1993 or he knew later that such a plan existed. According to the Trial Chamber, Slobodan Praljak shared the intent, along with other members of the JCE, the intent to permanently remove the Muslim population from the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. The Defence contends this conclusion because there is no evidence to support this. Nevertheless, from this intent, which is the only inference that the Trial Chamber -- of fact that the Trial Chamber established, Slobodan Praljak cannot be convicted on the basis of JCE for crimes against humanity because he can only be held reliable for crimes related to the displacement of the population. He should be -- his conviction could be -- should be annulled for all the other grounds. For such conviction to be possible, the Trial Chamber should have established that the crimes were within the framework of a common plan and that Slobodan Praljak shared, along with other members of the JCE, the intent of committing each of those crimes, but it did not do so. The Trial Chamber did not properly establish how Slobodan Praljak contributed to the common plan. It held that Slobodan Praljak facilitated and led the military operations in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 558. But the participation of the accused in military operations which are inherent to any armed conflict is not enough to hold an accused -- or to hold that an accused was contributing to a common plan. And besides, Slobodan Praljak's activities in Gornji Vakuf were aimed at easing the tension. The famous 15 January 1993 ultimatum was drafted in the night between 13 to 14 January 1993 in Zagreb, in the presence of Lord Owen, Cyrus Vance, and Alija Izetbegovic. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 475. Praljak went to Bosnia-Herzegovina at the joint request of President Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic, the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, P1739, 3D561. And the Trial Chamber acknowledged that Praljak was the envoy of President Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic. Volume 4, paragraph 534. The presence of two parties as well as representatives of the international community shows that the document was drafted without any criminal intent; on the contrary, in the hope that the conflict could be prevented. The Trial Chamber ignored the basic legal principles because it concluded that there was no specific information about the instructions that Praljak could have done to -- could have given to HVO. Judgement volume 4, paragraph 559. It held that Slobodan Praljak was involved in a common plan. And the situation was the same for Prozor, because the Trial Chamber could not find for Slobodan Praljak the requisite intent necessary for JCE 1. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 573. And once again, the Trial Chamber changed the positive actions of Slobodan Praljak aimed at preventing any criminal act into contributing to JCE. On 17 August 1993, Slobodan Praljak ordered that all prisoners be taken off labour. In other words, he forbade prisoners' labour, P4260. This order does not indicate that Slobodan Praljak knew that unlawful work was going on for prisoners since that, according to the Third Geneva Convention, prisoners' labour is not unlawful, as such. But against all odds, the Trial Chamber inferred from this document that Slobodan Praljak knew that prisoners were used for labour on the front line, which is indeed forbidden and prohibited. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 574. As for Mostar, Your Honour, I already said that the Trial Chamber held that he played no role, no role at all, in Mostar until 24 January -- July - sorry - 1993. The JCE is not an open-ended concept that allows for conviction by simple association. The accused that takes part in a JCE of course does not have to take part in the actus reus, but he must play a role; he must be involved in the implementation of the common plan. And the Trial Chamber held that Slobodan Praljak played no role, no role. With regard to the role that Slobodan Praljak played in Mostar after 24 July 1993, the Trial Chamber continued to change the evidence and to misinterpret them. It held that Slobodan Praljak ordered to get rid of Muslim terrorists in Mostar. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 579. Although getting rid of terrorists shouldn't take anyone by surprise, it's quite surprising that the Trial Chamber gave it some importance. And actually Slobodan Praljak's order was quite precise and specific; he ordered to eliminate terrorist groups of the Muslim armed forces. And this order was totally lawful and legitimate. With regard to the role that Slobodan Praljak played in Vares - and my learned friend will give you more details about this - the conclusions of the Trial Chamber are contradictory, confused, and not really clear. Judgement, volume 4, paragraphs 61 and 524. Once again, the Trial Chamber did not assess the evidence the way it should have done it by hastily concluding that Slobodan Praljak was contradicting himself and ignoring testimonies of Slobodan Praljak and Milivoje Petkovic that confirmed the same information. Judgement, volume 3, paragraph 324. The Trial Chamber made a series of errors with regard to the role that Slobodan Praljak played in the detention centres. The only thing that the Trial Chamber could establish was that Slobodan Praljak was willing to improve detention conditions, as well as his willingness to implement and enforce Geneva Conventions. Judgement, volume 4, paragraphs 602, 603, 607, 608, 611, and 612. In this situation where Slobodan Praljak was doing his utmost to implement the Geneva Conventions, the Trial Chamber could not establish the necessary mens rea in order to convict him for JCE 1, but it convicted Slobodan Praljak for crimes that would have been committed in the Dretelj and Gabela centres on the basis of JCE 1. And my colleague will give you further information if need be. There is no doubt that Slobodan Praljak was participating in the military activities of HVO between 24 July and 9 November 1993, because this was his duty over this period; but this is not enough to establish his contribution to the JCE. And the Trial Chamber should have established that Slobodan Praljak was acting and had the intent of pursuing the common plan - Tadic appeal judgement, paragraph 229 - and it did not do so. The method that the Trial Chamber applied led it to make an absurd finding, since the Trial Chamber ended up considering the positive actions that Slobodan Praljak undertook in order to ease the situation, to prevent crimes, to bring peace, and to alleviate civilians as a contribution to the common plan. Your Honours, war is no child's play. War is cruel and crimes are part of it. There is no such thing as a clean war. And as long as international law does not prohibit wars as such, crimes will be committed over their course. This doesn't mean that one should accept them and even less that the perpetrators shouldn't be convicted, but those who intended to commit them should be convicted. No one should be expected to do the impossible and throughout the whole war, Slobodan Praljak worked to end the convict. Throughout the war he fought against crimes, and some decisions he made required bravery in this context and at the time. He did what he could do and never had any criminal intent, not even a criminal thought. And by the way, the Trial Chamber could never establish that. So the Trial Chamber did not properly assess the evidence. It did not properly establish facts. It did not properly enforce law and did not give us any reasons for this decision. All we are asking for today is that the evidence is properly assessed in this case and that the applicable law be properly enforced for the properly established facts. I thank you for your attention. I now give the floor back to the lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Pinter, you have more or less three-quarters of an hour. We will stop at half past 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to try to finish within my time. Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm going to begin by replying to your questions. After that, I'm going to draw the attention of the Appeals Chamber to procedural and factual errors of the Trial Chamber that we referred to in our appeal which we consider to be exceptionally important due to the consequences they have had, which are that General Praljak did not have a fair trial. Dr. Prlic's Defence and Mr. Stojic's Defence responded to questions that you put to Defence counsel, and I join with their arguments and the answers to the questions that they gave. I'm going to discuss questions 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7. We have addressed all the legal and factual errors of the Trial Chamber regarding the elements of the crimes for which General Praljak, in relation to Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje was convicted, and we have covered those in our grounds of appeal 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15. We have stated our position in Ground 38 about the sustainability of conclusions regarding JCE 3. Question 3 that you have put has already been given an answer by the Defence of Mr. Stojic in their oral submissions. Here, I would just like to stay that the conclusion of the Trial Chamber was not explained in an understandable way as to the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that enabled the establishment of the intent to hurt or murder civilians. The Trial Chamber did not have these -- this evidence because the Prosecution did not present them, evidence which could justify such a conclusion. The Trial Chamber did not establish the preconceived plan and what its contents were, when, where, and with whom Slobodan Praljak planned the military operations; did he, when, and from whom did Slobodan Praljak receive any information regarding the particulars and the results of the conflict between the ABiH army and the HVO. In other words, did he know that civilians were killed in the combat operations in the village of Dusa? The Trial Chamber did not establish that the HVO fired the shell at the house on Enver Sljivo, and therefore it was not able to establish that the HVO had the requisite intent to inflict grave injuries and that he could have anticipated that civilians would be killed, the civilians who happened to be in the house of the commander of the ABiH unit. The Trial Chamber did not establish - it did not have evidence to that effect - that members of the HVO knew that there were civilians in the house of the ABiH army commander, a house which was located immediately next to a dug-in bunker, as shown in Exhibit 3D00527, P01213, and paragraph 359 of volume 2 of the judgement. There were 25 members, soldiers, of the BiH army in the bunker. There is no evidence, nor could it have reasonably been concluded, that the soldiers or members of the HVO in such a situation could have foreseen that there was civilians in an army commander's house. I also have to mention - and this is important in your assessment of the events in the village of Dusa - that the bunker which was next to the house in the village of Dusa, the house that belonged to the BiH army commander, fires were shot at members of the HVO; and this can be seen in exhibit 3D00527. It's a document dated the 16th of January, 1993, where it states that there were 25 soldiers of the BiH army. It also talks that the bunker was next to a large house, there was a dugout next to the house, and that there were fired shots from there too "at our boys." This is a quotation from a document. We have written in our grounds of appeal 12.2 about the intention to cause the death of civilians in the house of Enver Sljivo. I would just also like to say the following regarding question 3. The presence of the Croatian army in January 1993 was established through the fact that the soldiers who entered the village spoke Croatian. Exhibit P09202, Rule 92 statement by Enver Sljivo, who -- as my previous speakers have said, he was not subjected to a cross-examination. His statement was admitted as a written one, so he said that that was the Croatian army and he established this because they spoke Croatian, based on that fact. People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, particularly in Herzegovina, Croatian people, speak the same sort of Croatian spoken by Croats from Croatia. So the fact that a person or persons who entered a village spoke Croatian cannot be used as evidence of the presence of the Croatian army in the village of Dusa on the 18th of January, 1993. The specific error that the Trial Chamber committed regarding the charges for the village of Dusa is an error in law. My colleague Mr. Khan addressed this in his submissions, so I absolutely agree with his arguments. And now question number 4. Your question states: "If the Trial Chamber finding on the intent of HVO forces with regard to the deaths of civilians who had taken refuge in Enver Sljivo's house in the village of Dusa is overturned and if this finding that this incident constituted the crimes of murder and wilful killing are consequently reversed, the impact on the following." So what would it have -- what effect would it have on the common criminal purpose in terms of JCE 3? The position of the Defence is the following. In that case, the events in Gornji Vakuf cannot be considered as crimes under JCE and a common criminal plan. They should be viewed as an incident between the HVO and the BiH army at the municipal level due to disagreements between Croats and Muslims, which disagreements led to a conflict, which then did not spread to the entire area of the HZ HB, which should have happened if there had been a plan to cleanse the space and free it up for Croats by removing the Muslims. In order to have such a common criminal purpose, the conflict would have continued in other areas. However, following the 18th or the 22nd of January, when the conflicts in Gornji Vakuf ceased, there were no longer any more conflicts until later when the Army BiH began an offensive. In paragraph 45 of volume 4 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber concludes the following in relation to Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje. As the HZ HB leaders were participating in peace talks, the HVO conducted military campaigns in the provinces it considered Croatian in order to consolidate its presence here. I'm now quoting from the judgement. Consolidating presence cannot in any way be part of the implementation of any plan, particularly not if such an assertion is taken out of context. The Trial Chamber's conclusion does not follow from its reasoning and does not reply to the question why events in Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje are considered to be part of a common criminal plan. They do not answer the questions of when and how that plan was conceived. The position of the Defence in the proceedings and in the appeal is always the same: There was no JCE, there was no criminal plan. The real open and general war between the HVO and the BH army began in June 1993 when the BiH army offensive began in Central Bosnia, and then in September, along the valley of the Neretva River spreading to Herzegovina. In the course of the conflict between two armies of one state, crimes did occur. We never contested that. But they were not part of a criminal plan. Regrettably they were a consequence of the extraordinary and chaotic situation caused by war. As my learned friend said, crimes are part of war, unfortunately. The (b) part of the question, the mens rea of Praljak for murder under the first category of joint criminal enterprise. To that, the response -- the Defence provided its response in Ground 12, errors that relate to the military action in the village of Dusa. I emphasise here that the presence of members of the BiH army in the village of Dusa - with whom the HVO was in conflict from the 11th of January, not from the 18th of January - provides legitimacy to the military actions of the HVO. It was not unlawful and it was, in particular, not directed against the civilian population. If it were really a small number of BiH army soldiers or defenders of the village, as they are referred to in the judgement, then the conflict would not have lasted two days. It would have been completed in a much shorter period of time. The Trial Chamber did not have evidence through which it could establish that Praljak knew that there was civilians in the house of the BiH army commander. Therefore, he could not have the intent for killing. Also, there isn't a single exhibit that the Trial Chamber mentioned in its judgement based on which it would be able to conclude that Praljak could have known there was civilians in Enver Sljivo's house instead of members of the ABiH army. This is paragraph 342, volume 2 of the judgement. Thus, in a local conflict which Praljak tried to calm down - and we heard that from my colleague Ms. Fauveau - civilians were killed from a shell which we don't know who fired; the Trial Chamber did not establish that. Therefore, all available evidence does not provide the opportunity to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that Praljak intended for civilians to be killed, that he knew that there were civilians in the village, that he ordered that civilians be killed, that he in any way willingly, deliberately, or by omission caused the death of civilians who were in the house of the BiH army commander, next to which there was an entrenched unit of the BiH army which was firing at members of the HVO. Now we're talking about (c), which is part of question 4, and your question is the mens rea of Praljak for murder under the third category of joint criminal enterprise invites Praljak further to discuss along with other relevant evidence not on the trial record, if any, the significance of Zeljko Siljeg's report of 28 -- 29th January, 1993. This is Exhibit P01351. In relation to -- this is the position of the Defence in relation to JCE 3. We believe that if there is no JCE there can be no JCE 3 either. In responding to this question, we know that the analysis of available evidence does not permit a decision on Praljak's criminal intent: The intent to begin a conflict with the BiH army and, in particular, to commit crimes. Praljak could not have known, nor should he have known, nor could he have foreseen that murders would be committed. Exhibit P1351 is a report on the situation in Vakuf on the 28th of January, 1993; it was drafted after the conflicts stopped. A joint commission of the BiH army and the HVO established the effects of the conflict and the damage caused during the combat. That is what it says in the document. Two houses were damaged from shelling, were destroyed in the village of Uzricje; two houses were destroyed in the village of Dusa; and one house suffered minor damage in the village of Luzane. If there were a joint criminal plan, as stated in the judgement, one could then ask: Why would the HVO have a joint commission with the BiH army? Why would they establish the effects of the clash together, the damage caused? And why ultimately the civilians returned to their homes? If there was a common criminal plan to create a territory dominated by Croats, why were military operations halted? Why were Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje not captured when it was possible? And why attempt to jointly assess the consequences of the conflict at all? Additionally, the document also shows that there was no common criminal plan that would encompass the conflict in Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje since the document shows the following. I'm of the opinion that the question of Gornji Vakuf must be resolved as soon as possible and at a higher level, unilaterally or bilateral, because a single shot could re-trigger the war. Calling for a solution at a higher level at Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje shows without doubt that there was no common criminal plan or a JCE; because had it existed, the drafter of the document would not be asking that the issue of Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje be resolved at a higher level. Rather, they would militarily defeat the army by continuing military operation and would have captured Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje. In reference to the village of Dusa, an important fact from this document is that it was verified, that 23 soldiers were detained. These were not defenders of the village; these were soldiers of the BiH army, and that is why we do not accept the qualification of the Trial Chamber that these were village defenders. Also in the document there is another -- there were 23 soldiers there who were captured, and the Defence does not accept the qualification of the Trial Chamber that these were defenders of the village. The Defence asserts that these were members of the BiH army, regular soldiers. Another thing that the document states that is worthy of your attention is the fact that the author of the document states that somebody fired a recoilless gun at Enver Sljivo's house in which women and children were killed. The author of the document notes - and he is a member of the HVO - the following: "We did not have a recoilless gun." The Trial Chamber did not actually establish what type of artillery weapon fired the shell that had such a tragic result. General Praljak received information by the 22nd but he did not receive information in this document because on the 29th of January, 1993, was no longer in Gornji Vakuf. The document was not sent to him. He has no knowledge about the consequences of the armed conflict between the BiH army and the HVO in the village of Dusa. After facts are established, they are interpreted according to the law. For the sake of argument, because the Defence holds that JCE 3 does not exist at all, the JCE 3 mode of liability cannot be applied to the facts the Trial Chamber established in relation to death of civilians in the village of Dusa. And now my response to question 5. I am skipping some things because of a lack of time. The question states: "The basis for the Trial Chamber's finding that the property destruction caused during the attacks on the villages of Dusa, Hrasnica, Zdrimci, and Uzricje was wanton and not justified by military necessity and whether there would be any effect if this finding were overturned on the finding that the property destruction caused during attacks on several localities in Gornji Vakuf municipality was extensive." The conclusions of the Trial Chamber that the destruction of property during the attack on the villages of Dusa, Hrasnica, Zdrimci, and Uzricje was wanton and not justified by military necessity are not based on the evidence. The Trial Chamber had evidence that in the area of Gornji Vakuf, Uskoplje municipality, there were incidents, conflicts, between the HVO and the BiH army that in said places and facilities there were members of the BiH army who took an active part in the conflict. That on the 11th of January and the 12th of January, 1993, conflicts began between the BiH army and the HVO, and they occurred in the villages of Dusa, Hrasnica, Zdrimci, and Uzricje on those dates. This is volume 2, paragraph 336 of the trial judgement. In the same paragraph the Trial Chamber notes that Serbian forces also participated in the conflict, but the Trial Chamber did not establish what the damage was that was inflicted by members of the HVO. The Trial Chamber did not establish who and when -- damaged the property. This is volume 2, paragraph 352. The Defence holds that the only conclusion -- the Defence holds that it was not established beyond a reasonable doubt that the destruction of property was excessive, as it was not established that the destruction of property was wilful. It could not have been established that it was excessive. We dealt with this in Ground 11 of our appeal. I would like to ask the interpreters to say when I say Gornji Vakuf, Uskoplje, for them to write Gornji Vakuf, Uskoplje, because that is it the official name of the town or the village. Response to question 6 as to whether the evidence with particular reference to Exhibits P06068 and P06073 establishes that Praljak knew that UNPROFOR was seeking access to Stupni Do between the 23rd and the 25th of October, 1993, and that he sought to prevent such access -- that Praljak sought to prevent such access. This is a question to be dealt with by the Defence of Praljak and the OTP. In order to answer this properly, I would like to ask for a closed session, since I'm going to be dealing with documents under seal and with allegations made during closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's go in closed session, please. Wait, wait, wait. Wait. We are not yet in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document P6073 is information Milivoje Petkovic is sending to Slobodan Praljak to the Main Staff of the HVO in Citluk. From the document General Praljak learns that the UN is requesting the transfer of 45 tonnes of explosives from the Sarajevo airport and about 25.000 detonators allegedly for the construction of a road in the Kakanj sector. "I am concerned that this might be intended for the Muslims. Serbs for now are not allowing them permission for in transport." Among other things the information says: "Firing by our side chased the UN away. I'm trying to reverse the situation." This is a document from the 25th of October, 1993. General Praljak does not find out from this document that the UN is seeking access to Stupni Do, but he does find out that UN is asking to transfer large quantities of explosives. Document P6068 also from the 25th of October, 1993, is signed by General Praljak and it is a -- evidently response from questions from document P6073. Item 3 of the document says that the UN request for the transfer of explosives should not be allowed until further notice through our territory and that Milivoje Petkovic should do everything to show that we did not chase the UN away from Vares. So there is nothing there about Stupni Do and preventing the entrance to Stupni Do. Praljak did not find out that UNPROFOR sought access to Stupni Do. General Praljak on the 25th of October, 1993, didn't even know that there was a crime committed in Stupni Do. Volume 4, paragraph 641 of the judgement. As for relations with UNPROFOR, Slobodan Praljak evidently approved of the actions of Petkovic directed at -- rectifying the situation in relation to UNPROFOR. Document D6063 is an order by Milivoje Petkovic on the 24th of October, 1993, at 2315 hours. It is sent to the commander of the Bobovac Brigade, requesting that all activities towards UNPROFOR cease and that UNPROFOR must be given unimpeded access and movement so there is no possibility here, either by Praljak or Petkovic, to restrict movement by UNPROFOR. Exhibit P06078 is a request sent from the Main Staff of the HVO, Milivoje Petkovic, on the 25th of October, 1993, to the commander of the Bobovac Brigade and Ivica Rajic, asking to have information, true information, about Stupni Do submitted by 9.00 the next morning. So they don't know what happened in Stupni Do. Therefore, the response to your question is that General Praljak did not know that UNPROFOR was being prevented from accessing Stupni Do, that he did not know that crimes were committed. Therefore, regarding Stupni Do, his responsibility cannot be accepted. Again, I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have eight minutes left. You have eight minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask to have an extra two minutes, perhaps -- ah, perhaps it is because of the tape. I did lose some time still. Would I be able to have a little bit of extra time after the break perhaps, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm actually informed that we have only seven minutes of tape left, so you have to stop after seven minutes. I'll confer with my colleagues to see if we can give you an extra three minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be possible to have some time after the break? Three minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Yes, while we're discussing the time, could I make one request or suggestion. If indeed General Praljak is going to make submissions at some point in the scope of the appeal, could I suggest that rather than it be -- being done during the reply time, if he could just use some of their reply time in response then, if necessary, it would enable the Prosecution to then respond to whatever submissions he makes as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I can't create -- review the schedule. What my suggestion is, if Madam Pinter requires an extra five minutes, we can grant her five minutes after the break before you start. And then have you an extra five minutes when we reconvene. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I lost my place, but my time is running, so very well. I'm going to end with question 6. It's all stated in our appeal submission anyway, so I'm not answering to the end. Then question 7 regarding Gabela and Dretelj. I will shorten by saying that there is not a single piece of evidence in the case file which would beyond a reasonable doubt establish that General Praljak knew about the conditions in Gabela and Dretelj; but what I would like to stress more is that General Praljak was not obliged in any way to know about the conditions in Gabela and Dretelj because he was the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO. He was conducting military operations. He was saving the lives of Croats who were attacked in Central Bosnia and along the Neretva River Valley. There's no piece of evidence on file indicating that there exists any single document pertaining to Dretelj and Gabela that was sent to the Main Staff or to General Praljak. Therefore, the conclusion that he was aware of the conditions and circumstances prevailing at Dretelj and Gabela is completely untenable. If I need to stop now, I will gladly do so and continue after the tapes have been switched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have the break now. We will reconvene at 12.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the decision is, madam, you will conclude later on this afternoon, during the reply section; and Mr. Praljak will make his intervention now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you have ten minute, Mr. Praljak, not more. THE APPELLANT PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. It concerns a document pertaining to the joint comment of the ABiH and the HVO of the 15th of January, 1993. Given the fact that I testified before this Court, this document was drafted in co-operation with Mr. Izetbegovic in Zagreb on the 13th and 14th of January, 1993. The Trial Chamber omitted to ascribe any sense or importance to the document, and whatever importance they assigned to it was mistaken. The HVO and the ABiH were equal components of the armed forces of the BH. They had to have joint commands. They had to. To continue. In that document, the ABiH and the HVO, the two components of the BiH armed forces, are mirror reflections of each other in terms of treatment. If two parties are treated in such a way, no party can issue ultimatums to the other. That is basic logic. I further assert the following. Unless there are joint commands between two armed forces that act as partners and allies, there is no way to avoid individual or extensive clashes between two such armed forces. The non-existence of joint command will eventually lead to a military defeat of such an armed force against the enemy, but clashes were unavoidable because the non-existence of joint commands was an architectural mistake within the system of alliance as it existed. The document was created based on certain assertions I made as well, because I took part in its design and drafting. As a sociologist, at least for a period of my life, I studied the history of warfare. War is the most disastrous aspect of human civilisation and society. From Thucydides, von Clausewitz and others on. I tried to find the answers to the causes and consequences of the concept of war and how it affects society, starting with myself, of course, and the concept of war in and of itself. I wanted to find the answer to the question of who wins or loses a war and for what reason. Your Honours, I didn't find a single example, a single case, in which two or more allied armed forces would function without a joint command. Joint commands are sine quo non of the functioning of allied armies. Joint commands are the alphabet, the basic prerogative of any alliance of armed forces. Why is that so? War is governed by fear unless there is a possibility to resolve individual conflicts, armed forces located at front lines without communication, with arms in their hands, the appearance of mistrust is imminent or unavoidable, that one would turn on the other, that there they allow the enemy through the backdoor and so on and so forth. All of that breeds fear, and under such circumstances armies cannot function. An example of that is the fall of Jajce in 1992. Even to this day arguments are exchanged in terms of who was the first one to leave the front line facing the Serb forces. There was no joint command. The HVO was afraid that the ABiH soldiers would be the first ones to leave and vice versa. The population saw there was something wrong and started to flee. The soldiers representing the particular community see their population leave and they leave themselves. Therefore, everybody flees ultimately and the issue of who fled first becomes irrelevant. It happens everywhere and all the time. Let us look at the joint command functioning during the invasion in Normandy in 1944 and the Allied Forces. There was a joint command. Dwight Eisenhower was the joint commander, but did not draft orders to -- the American divisions were commanded by Bradley, the British divisions by Montgomery. They simply co-ordinated. They discussed who went how far, whose flank was exposed, and who needed air support. All other attributes that comprise an armed force, such as arming, logistics, rotation of commanders fall within the ambit of individual armed forces. Joint commands do not become involved in that. If there is no joint command, necessarily it will lead to a conflict starting at an individual level and up. If there is no forum to deal with it, if there is no joint command which would increase trust, tour the front lines, visit the soldiers, such an armed force cannot survive. Experiments conducted by social psychologists show that conflicts of amorphus groups caused by irrelevant causes continue for months even once those involved learn that the conflict was intended. War is governed by fear, the fear of being abandoned, the fear of being caught unawares, or of being killed. When this document was being drafted, the gist of was it that it was not an ultimatum. It was a necessary requisite so as to avoid any conflict. The document was supposed to go to Sarajevo to be used by the ABiH the same way the HVO used it. To conclude, by refusing the proposal on joint commands was a clear indication, a clear message that somebody did not want to be an ally, that somebody was intending to attack. In and of itself such decision is evil and it testifies to the basic belief of eventually conducting offensive operation against your temporary ally, which is exactly what happened in the ensuing months. Unable to oppose the Army of Republika Srpska, the ABiH and the Muslim political leadership attacked the HVO and the Croats so as to compensate for the territories lost. All evidence points to that. The so-called JCE, as stipulated by the judgement and those involved, throughout the period following the 15th of January sent and kept sending all the necessary arms to the ABiH as well as equipment. Ninety per cent of the overall military arsenal at the disposal of the ABiH during the war was obtained through -- or by -- by the Croats. All evidence indicates that was the case. Thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Thank you. Mr. Stringer, are you ready to go? Or do you prefer Ms. Pinter to make her ten-minute submission now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's fine with the Prosecution either way, I think is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed, start, because it will get -- there's very little time left in any case and I suppose it's wiser to go like I'm suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Then with that, I will be making the Prosecution submissions in response to the submissions of General Praljak, and in the course of that I'll be responding to Your Honours' questions 4(c) as well as question 8 as they relate to General Praljak, question 8 relating to his specific intent to spread terror. And I will also be making the Prosecution response on question 2 regarding the Old Bridge. My colleague, Ms. Finnin, after I'm finished, probably after the lunch break will be making the Prosecution's submissions in response to your questions 6 and 7 on Stupni Do and the detention camps. Your Honours have already heard submissions yesterday and on Monday from my colleagues, Ms. Gustafson, Ms. Goy in relation to occupation, international armed conflict and the conflict in Gornji Vakuf, specifically the questions -- the Chamber's question in relation to Dusa. And our submissions, we adopt those as our own submissions in relation to appellant General Praljak, Mr. President, with just a few brief exceptions for clarifications, some additions, supplements, we'd like to make today in response to what's been said already by my friends on General Praljak's Defence. In regard to occupation, there was an assertion that the HVO forces, the Bosnian Croats, could not occupy those parts of Herceg-Bosna and we just wanted -- it's in our submissions but just to make it perhaps more clear. By arguing that the HVO could not occupy parts of BiH, the Defence overlooks that this is an occupation by agency as was found by the Trial Chamber and that Croatia is the occupying power here, and, of course, Croatia could indeed be an occupying power in relation to parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Croatia's role as an occupying power is -- I refer Your Honours to volume 1, paragraph 96, and to volume 3, footnote 1175 of the Trial Chamber judgement in relation to that point. And then just a couple of follow-up in response to submissions earlier about the HVO attack on the village of Dusa which forms part of the Chamber's questions 3 and 4. Today the Defence argued that there was significant fighting in Dusa, and relying on a finding that the HVO took control of Dusa after one or two days of fighting, the Defence relied on volume 2, paragraph 365. But, Your Honours, when you look at the underlying evidence, it is clear that the HVO took control of Dusa in less than a day. The attack on Dusa began in earnest on the morning of the 18th of January. The HVO took control of the village and detained all its inhabitants, defenders and civilians alike, that afternoon. And for this we refer you to the evidence of Kemal Sljivo, Exhibit P10108, pages 3 to 4, and the testimony of Witness BW at transcript page 780. On the assertion we heard today, Your Honours, that the Trial Chamber did not establish that the HVO fired the shell that hit the Sljivo house, we say that in fact in volume 3, paragraphs 663 and 711, the Chamber clearly found the HVO was responsible for the shelling of Enver Sljivo's house and the finding's amply supported by the evidence you've heard the Prosecution refer to on Monday. Finally the Defence said that the HVO could not have foreseen that there were civilians in Enver Sljivo's house and they rely on the fact that the house belonged to the commander of the village defence. As you heard from my colleague on Monday, Ms. Gustafson, Your Honours, a residential house -- it's our position a residential house is a prima facie civilian object. There was no indication here that it was being used for a military purpose, no defenders were in the house, no shots were fired from the house, and a house that was obviously occupied with smoke rising from the chimney. The Defence seems to be repeating the claim that they made in the brief that the mere fact that the owner of Sljivo's house was among the local defenders was itself a justification for the HVO to target the house despite the absence of any military activity associated with the house. And as we've said in our submissions, Your Honours, on Monday, we say that in fact when they attacked the house on such circumstances, it was at the very least an indiscriminate attack. With that said, Your Honour -- oh, let me just go, first of all, to another couple of the points that were made earlier today. One of those relates to General Praljak's challenges to the Trial Chamber's findings on the ultimate purpose. And here we would refer Your Honours back primarily to the Trial Chamber's findings on the ultimate purpose, leading to the ultimate purpose, which are set out in paragraphs 6 to 24 of volume 4 and as well as to the Prosecution's submissions that were made on Monday. I made those submissions, Your Honours. I hope, I tried to, as clearly as I am able to, lead Your Honours through the Chamber's findings on ultimate purpose and how well supported they are by the evidence. Issues relating to the plan, the aspiration, the obsession, as was said by Mr. Karnavas on Monday, of President Tudjman to restore the Banovina and how that required the use of crimes inside Herceg-Bosna territory in order to achieve that ultimate purpose? We commend Your Honours to the testimony of Ambassador Galbraith, I referred to it on Monday, we'll be coming back to it today, as well as to the testimony of Ambassador Okun, who the Chamber relies on extensively among all its findings regarding ultimate purpose. It's Ambassador Okun that speaks to the two-track policy, what he considered to be a two-track policy. This relates to other submissions made here today, Your Honours, in relation to Croatia'S alleged benign intentions in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, sending arms to the ABiH, the so-called -- well, the agreement on friendship and co-operation between the HVO and the ABiH which has also been referred to. None of that undermines the Chamber's findings, the core fundamental findings on the existence of the joint criminal enterprise as applied to this case, this conflict between those two armed forces. And nothing called an agreement on friendship and co-operation is going to undermine or cast doubt on the fact that there was a very brutal war taking place during the period here, 1993 and 1994, between these two military forces, the HVO and the ABiH.
