Croatia, as Your Honours know, because all of you have sat on Chambers in cases involving events taking place in the north of Bosnia, the east of Bosnia during this period, 1993, 1994, you know that there was a very strong conflict between the Serbs, the VRS on one side, and unified Croat and Muslim forces that were fighting against the Serbs. It was in Croatia's interest to support those efforts and that involved providing supplies to Muslim fighters in other parts of the country. It was in Croatia's interest to do so. But none of that undermines the basic ultimate findings here that when we look at the conflict that we're concerned with here, the conflict between the ABiH and the HVO in Herceg-Bosna, there wasn't anything benign about Croatia's intentions and there wasn't anything involving friendship and co-operation. Your Honours, many of Slobodan Praljak's arguments were made at the trial, they were rejected by the Trial Chamber after extensive detailed findings on Praljak's role in developing the JCE before January 1993 and then contributing to its implementation throughout the claimed territories of Herceg-Bosna until the 9th of November, 1993, when he quit the HVO and Bosnia-Herzegovina altogether to return to Croatia. The final destruction of the Old Bridge, the Stari Most, and its collapse into the Neretva River on that day, the 9th of November, is emblematic of the destruction and the misery that he left behind. As he did at trial, Praljak claims on appeal that he was just a simple soldier. We see this in his brief at paragraph 385. In fact, as the Trial Chamber rightly concluded, Praljak was one of the most important members of the joint criminal enterprise. He exercised significant de facto and, later, de jure and de facto authority over the HVO armed forces and its military police. That's volume 4, paragraph 1340. In considering the evidence proving Praljak's high-level positions in the Croatian government and the role he played as President Tudjman's advisor and agent in the BiH, the Trial Chamber concluded that Praljak enjoyed a "privileged and continuous link" to Croatia's leadership on subjects regarding BiH and Croatia's engagement there. That's volume 4, paragraph 1223. Praljak, Your Honours, was no simple soldier. As the Trial Chamber found, and it's not in dispute, throughout 1992 and much of 1993, Slobodan Praljak was an Assistant Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. His superior was co-JCE member, Defence Minister Gojko Susak. Praljak was a member of Croatia's national Security Council, the VONS, and he was a trusted advisor to Tudjman. He was also a major-general in the Croatia army. Prior to the 24th of July, 1993, he was all of these things while simultaneously exercising de facto authority over the HVO armed forces on the ground in Herceg-Bosna, armed forces that committed crime on a large scale. On the 24th of July, 1993, Praljak officially assumed command over the HVO armed forces, including its military police, as commander of the HVO Main Staff. Even then he remained on Croatia's payroll. See volume 4, paragraph 520. It's the combination of these high-level positions held by Praljak prior to and during the JCE that made him one of its most important members and enabled him to participate both in the development and the implementation of the criminal plan to change the ethnic makeup of Herceg-Bosna. In my submissions this morning, Your Honours, this afternoon, I should say, I will address Praljak's challenges in Grounds 39 and 41 to the Trial Chamber's findings regarding his awareness of the common criminal plan and his shared intent. I will then address his challenges to the Chamber's findings on two aspects of his contribution to the JCE, his role as a conduit between Croatia and Herceg-Bosna, and his use of HVO forces to commit crimes in furtherance of the common criminal plan in such places as Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, and Mostar as set out in his Ground 40. In Ground 39, Praljak claims that the Trial Chamber erred when it considered his pre-JCE conduct. And this was raised earlier this morning by my colleague in relation to their oral submissions, consideration of his acts prior to the beginning of the joint criminal enterprise. We rely -- the Chamber in fact relied on things Praljak said and did during 1992 in high-level meetings with Croatia's leadership and in secret meetings with VRS commander Ratko Mladic, and they did this when considering his awareness of the common plan. In fact, the Chamber's consideration of this pre-JCE conduct amply establishes that he played a key role in developing the common plan and that he shared the intent once implementation began in January of 1993. It is well settled, Your Honours, in our jurisprudence that an accused's pre-JCE conduct may be considered in relation to a variety of important issues once the JCE does come into being, such as an accused's role in the JCE and his mens rea. In the Djordjevic appeal judgement, paragraph 297, the Appeals Chamber observed that an accused's pre-JCE meetings with senior political and military leaders could be considered for that purpose. And this is precisely what the Trial Chamber did here. See volume 4, paragraphs 18, 522, 525, 545. Praljak's conduct in the lead-up to the JCE tells us a great deal about his mens rea. In his acts and words, Praljak promoted ethnic separation, the division of BiH and reconstituting the borders of the 1939 Banovina territory. In other words, he promoted the ultimate purpose. What's more, he knew that achieving that would require changing the ethnic composition of this new Banovina territory in BiH called Herceg-Bosna through ethnic cleansing. On the 26th of September, 1992, Praljak raised the alarm with President Tudjman in a meeting of the VONS, the national Defence Council, in reference to Muslim refugees now living in areas inhabited by Croats. Lamenting the arrival of the refugees, Praljak observed that expulsions would be necessary in order to achieve a Croat-majority population. Your Honours have a slide, these are Praljak's words: "As things stand now, and with the kind of settlements we are seeing in Travnik, and areas to the south of Travnik, I am afraid that at the moment the war ends, in light of the substantial changes in the ethnic structure, our chances are slim, unless we decide to deal with this with them in another war, and this is what will happen, civil, international rights, et cetera." And he says: "It will be difficult to make those people leave those parts in any way," I think we have got a typo in our slide "... those parts in any way ... unless we evict those people from there we will not have a majority there." Unless we evict those people we will not have a majority. Although is he referring here to incoming Muslim refugees, we know that once implementation of the common criminal plan started in January of 1993, implementation was not limited to evicting only Muslim refugees. This JCE was about removing long-established Muslim populations in communities from large areas of Herceg-Bosna to create the necessary ethnic balance. Your Honours heard my reference on Monday and my colleague Mr. Menon's reference yesterday to the changed ethnic structure in Stolac when it was all said and done by September 1993. 8.000 Muslims down to 0. Stolac had been a Muslim majority municipality before the conflict. Nor did the Trial Chamber err when it considered Praljak's pre-JCE meetings with Ratko Mladic. Just ten days after this meeting we saw, the September 26th meeting between Praljak and President Tudjman, Praljak, together with Prlic, Stojic, travelled to Hungary where they had a secret meeting with VRS commander Ratko Mladic. This was referred to already, Your Honours, just to repeat. It was at this meeting that Praljak described the objective: "The goal is the Banovina of 1939; if not, we'll continue the war." That's Exhibit P11377, page 2, referred to at volume 4 -- sorry, 376 referred to at volume 4, paragraph 118. Paragraph 18. Bear in mind, Your Honours, that at this meeting Praljak was representing Croatia as an Assistant Minister of Defence. His reference to the Banovina obviously reflects the policy of Croatian President Tudjman. You've heard this about in our submissions on Monday. But it also bears on his knowledge and intent once the pattern of crimes is unleashed to implement it. In considering Praljak's knowledge and mens rea, how could the Trial Chamber ignore Praljak's statements to Mladic when they met again three weeks later, on the 26th of October, 1992. Praljak was again accompanied by Prlic and Stojic, joined also this time by Milivoje Petkovic. It was at this meeting that Praljak announced: "We're on a good path to compel Alija," that's a reference to Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic "to divide Bosnia." Later in this meeting he referred to the population movements he envisioned as part of the Herceg-Bosna plan: "It is our interest that the Muslims get their own canton so they have somewhere to move to." Volume 4, paragraphs 14 and 18. That's P11380. As with his statement to Mladic advocating the Banovina, Praljak's statement here about the Muslims having their own canton to move to reflects what was Croatian policy. Tudjman had referred to this concept in December of 1991 in an important meeting he had with Bosnian Croat leaders. Praljak attended the meeting. At the meeting, Tudjman referred to the creation of a "statelet" for Muslims in BiH which would serve as a "buffer zone in the demarcation of Serbia and Croatia." That's Exhibit P89, page 33. And the Chamber considers that meeting in volume 1, paragraph 428. In these examples, Praljak's statements to President Tudjman and to Ratko Mladic, we see Praljak advocating the essential elements, aspects of the ultimate purpose that led to the JCE that was launched in January of 1993: establishment of a Banovina territory, establishment of ethnically Croat majorities inside it, the outward movement of Muslims "to their own canton" to achieve this. The Trial Chamber properly considered Praljak's pre-JCE conversations with Tudjman and Mladic in relation to the JCE, his knowledge, and his mens rea. In any event, Praljak's advocacy of the Herceg-Bosna project did not end once the JCE started. The Trial Chamber noted in volume 4, paragraph 522: "From April 1992 to November 1993, Slobodan Praljak participated in meetings of the senior Croatian leadership at which Croatia's policy in BiH was discussed and defined with a view to furthering the common criminal purpose." And Your Honours will note in the judgement the Trial Chamber referred to numerous of the presidential transcripts, numerous conversations occurring at the presidential palace, numerous statements of Praljak, confirming that he was involved throughout the course of the JCE in advancing this policy. The Trial Chamber committed no error in considering all of Praljak's statements both prior to and during the JCE in finding that he shared the common plan to recreate the Banovina on BiH territory. His arguments to the contrary should be dismissed. Shared intent. This is largely Praljak's Ground 41. It has come up today. Praljak did not merely advocate the goal of changing the ethnic composition of Herceg-Bosna. He also shared the intent to use criminal means to achieve the goal. He intended a range of crimes, ranging from attacks on towns and villages, violent eviction operations, the unlawful detention and mistreatment of Muslim inhabitants of Herceg-Bosna. In his comments earlier, just a few moments ago, General Praljak made references to populations fleeing war. Your Honours, you're going to, we submit, find as the Trial Chamber did -- you're not going to find, you're going to, we submit, reasonably conclude that the Chamber reasonably concluded that every one of these crime bases that we've got in this case is one that is not about populations fleeing war. It's about deliberate attempts to drive a particular ethnic entity out, whether it's West Mostar evictions, whether it's the Muslim community removed from Stolac, Capljina, Ljubuski, whether it's eviction operations and destruction that occurred in the wake of, after attack operations, after the villages had been consolidated by the HVO. This is the pattern and the theme that runs throughout the entire case, and it's not about self-defence and it's not about people fleeing the ravages of war. As this implementation of the JCE unfolded throughout 1993 and the pattern of crimes revealed the goal of removing the Muslims, Praljak's actions reflect his intent. Although he didn't directly contribute to every single crime that was committed during the implementation of the JCE, he intended those crimes be used to implement it and he willingly played his part. This is what brings us to Praljak's contributions to the JCE. I'll now address additional aspects of Ground 40, where Praljak claims errors in the Trial Chamber's findings on his contribution to the JCE. In sub-Ground 40.1, he claims the Chamber's findings are too vague, requiring him to speculate as to their meaning. Praljak overlooks the careful analysis of the evidence of his unique and multi-faceted contributions set out in paragraphs 512 to 623 of volume 4. It is not vague. The Trial Chamber states precisely how Praljak contributed to the JCE. First, he contributed by serving as a conduit between Croatia and Herceg-Bosna to further the common criminal purpose. Volume 4, paragraph 545. By exercising his Croatia and Herceg-Bosna functions simultaneously, Praljak knew that the Herceg-Bosna policy -- he knew the Herceg-Bosna policy and willingly implemented it by transmitting orders and instructions from Croatia. He informed Croatia's leadership about the situation in BiH, Croatia's military support for the HVO armed forces. See volume 4, paragraphs 515, 545. Second, Praljak exercised de facto command authority over the HVO armed forces from the autumn of 1992 until the 24th of July, 1993. And then from that date until his departure on the 9th of November, Praljak had command and control authority and effective control over all components of the HVO as the commander of its HVO Main Staff. That's volume 4, paragraphs 482, 506, 624. He contributed to crimes by actively planning and directing operations of HVO units in which many crimes were committed. He contributed to the crimes committed by the HVO forces in Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Mostar, including the siege of East Mostar and Vares as well. Volume 4, paragraphs 546 to 598. The third contribution as found by the Trial Chamber was that despite his position at the apex of the political and military structures of Croatia and Herceg-Bosna during this period, his command over HVO forces, his privileged and continuous ties to Croatia's leadership, Slobodan Praljak did virtually nothing to stop or prevent crimes of his HVO subordinates. That's volume 4, paragraphs 617 to 623. As you'll hear from my colleague Ms. Finnin later, he works to block or stall UNPROFOR personnel from gaining access to Stupni Do after the HVO massacre there, and he worked with Petkovic to cover it up. He made no significant effort to improve the HVO's prisons at Gabela and Dretelj, even after news of the appalling conditions there become an international scandal. I will address Praljak's claims regarding the first two of these contributions, conduit and contribution to crimes as HVO commander. Regarding the role of conduit, I've already referred to Praljak's role in his meetings with Croatia's leadership as well as with VRS Commander Mladic in relation to his mens rea and his membership in the JCE. This does, of course, shed light on the nature of his role as a conduit after the JCE began. But let me take a few minutes first to address another key aspect of Praljak's conduit role: Delivering the message and the policy from Zagreb to those responsible for implementing the policy in Herceg-Bosna. I'll give you four illustrations. There's perhaps no better illustration of this than the role Praljak played in relation to the Prlic ultimatum. This set the stage for implementation of the JCE at Gornji Vakuf in January of 1993. I'm referring of course to the 15 January 1993 decision by Jadranko Prlic demanding that the ABiH units in Vance-Owen provinces attributed to Croats subordinate themselves to the HVO. And let me digress just a little bit here from my outline, Your Honours, to respond directly to some of the assertions that have been made by the Defence today. General Praljak referred Your Honours to his testimony at the trial in which he claimed that, in fact, he was delivering the essence of an agreement that had been reached in Zagreb between him, the Croatian leadership and Bosnian president, President Izetbegovic. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber had that evidence and they correctly did not credit that version of the events. When he was asked about this agreement that had been reached in Zagreb, the agreement in which the ABiH would subordinate itself to the HVO in these areas, whether the agreement had ever been put into writing, Praljak said, no, it was actually not ever a written agreement. It was what he called a gentlemen's agreement. So that's worth bearing in mind when considering whether such an agreement really came into an existence. The Chamber doesn't refer to this as an agreement anywhere in its findings. It correctly refers to this as an ultimatum. It was a unilateral ultimatum and it was based upon the HVO's misinterpretation, deliberate misinterpretation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. In my remarks on Monday I referred to the evidence, the testimony of Ambassador Okun who was one of the drafters, lead negotiators of the Vance-Owen Plan. He testified at trial that it was illegal; their interpretation was wrong and illegal. Also today my colleagues have referred to Exhibits P1739 and 3D561, asserting that in fact Praljak played a role as an envoy in respect of this matter. We responded to this argument in our brief and we refer Your Honours to that. What the Trial Chamber reasonably found, Your Honours, was that Praljak actively participated in drafting this ultimatum. We know he was involved in it. We disagree as to whether it was an ultimatum or an agreement. The Chamber's finding on that is the reasonable one. Praljak was in Mostar with Prlic, Stojic, and Petkovic on the 15th of January. Volume 4, paragraph 475. Once Prlic issued the ultimatum in Mostar, it then moved down the HVO chain of command through Stojic and Petkovic and then the HVO operative zones. In the days that followed, Praljak, who again was still an assistant minister of defence and a major-general in the Croatian army at this time, Praljak was present in the Gornji Vakuf region and he was active in implementing the Prlic ultimatum. This is at volume 4, paragraph 553, 556. In a few moments I'll talk more about Praljak's contributions to the crimes then that unfolded in Gornji Vakuf after the deadline on implementation of this ultimatum passed and the HVO attacked the villages in the municipality in Gornji Vakuf. Another example of Praljak's role as a conduit is his meeting on the 2nd of April, 1993, in which he carried the message of Croatian policy to HVO armed forces and military police in BiH. There he chaired a meeting of HVO authorities and commanders of the HVO Central Bosnia operative zone. Consistent with the views he had expressed in his earlier conversations with Tudjman and Mladic, Praljak spoke of population movements, the importance of creating a Croatian state within BiH. His co-JCE member Valentin Coric was present, together with HZ HB Vice-President Dario Kordic also convicted in this Tribunal. At this meeting, Praljak states: "Now we have got what we want. The homogenisation of our population continues. We can only fence off what is ours and build there our own space and our own state. It is all as clear as noon on a spring day." That's from Exhibit P1788. The Trial Chamber rightly considered these remarks to HVO personnel in Herceg-Bosna as illustrating both Praljak's role of conduit and his state of mind. Volume 4, paragraphs 532, 1343. Praljak claims in Ground 40 that he did not attend this meeting in an official capacity. That is not reasonable. See his appeal brief paragraph 438. As the Chamber noted, on the day of this meeting Praljak was an assistant minister of defence of Croatia, he was a major-general in its armed forces. His authority emanated from his privileged and continuous ties to the Croatian leadership. Also on this day, Praljak had de facto command authority over the HVO's own forces. He was addressing his subordinates, and the exhibit has him down as the person chairing the meeting. Okay, one more illustration, Mr. President, or is it time for the break? Looks like we've got about five minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You still have about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. President Tudjman himself saw Praljak as a surrogate and an implementer in Herceg-Bosna. The Trial Chamber relied on the transcript of the meeting at the presidential palace in Zagreb on the 2nd of July, 1993. Your Honours saw this yesterday, I believe, in Mr. Menon's submissions. After expressing concern about the possibility of international sanctions against Croatia for its support of the HVO, Tudjman instructed Susak and Bobetko as follows. Tudjman states: "But at the same time we must take steps to protect Croatian interests in the territorial sense too. And you two, please, Minister Susak, General Bobetko, see about this and meet with Herceg-Bosna leaders there, with General Praljak, Petkovic ... with Boban and Prlic, to discuss exactly what should be done. But, it goes without saying, do not lead the operation in such a way as to make a direct involvement." My colleague Mr. Menon referred to this yesterday in relation to the JCE membership of Mr. Susak and General Bobetko. This is another point that was raised in the submissions of my learned friend this morning. Your Honours will note that at this point in time, Praljak held no official position within the HVO. Tudjman is referring to his Assistant Minister of Defence here as a Herceg-Bosna leader. And it's correct: Praljak was both. It's also worth noting that when Tudjman issued these instructions to consult with Praljak and the others on taking steps to protect Croatian interests in the territorial sense, the HVO had already committed extensive crimes in its operations in Gornji Vakuf and Jablanica. The HVO personnel including military police were committing numerous crimes against the captive Muslim population in Prozor, the violent expulsions from West Mostar into East Mostar were in full swing, the JCE had by this time expanded to encompass crimes linked to the siege of East Mostar, terror and unlawful attacks. Two weeks after this meeting, Praljak would become the Herceg-Bosna leader -- I should say, two weeks after this meeting, Praljak would then become the commander of the HVO Main Staff, making official his position as a Herceg-Bosna leader. With that, Your Honours, if now is the time for a break, it's a good time for me to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. Mr. Stringer, you have spoken for 41 minutes so that you can calculate what time, the amount of time you have left. We will reconvene at half past 2.00. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.58 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we start, can I just say that Mr. Ellis before the break left the courtroom and our pro bono legal assistant, Ms. Molly Martin, is in court. Just for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. And for the record also -- I intended to do this earlier but I didn't. For the record, Mr. Karnavas came into the -- entered the courtroom while Mr. Praljak was addressing the Court. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, before the break we were addressing aspects of the Chamber's findings regarding Praljak's contribution as a conduit as between Croatia and the policies and events in Herceg-Bosna. And the last point I wanted to make on that is to draw Your Honours' attention to the Chamber's finding to the extent it was based upon Mr. Praljak's own testimony at trial, this finding that he played a role as a conduit between Croatia and Herceg-Bosna. When it was put to him on cross-examination that he was implementing President Tudjman's policies in Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Praljak replied: "No, I was implementing the policies of the Croatian state. My policies were parallel to the policies of the Republic of Croatia and the policies of Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, Bruno Stojic, Jadranko Prlic, and all the others." That's at pages 43001 to 43002 of the transcript referred to by the Chamber in volume 4, paragraph 527. Your Honours, the policy, as the Chamber found, was to change the ethnic composition of Herceg-Bosna through ethnic cleansing of Muslims. And as Praljak tells us in his own words at the trial, his contribution was to implement that policy. I'd like to now move to the Chamber's findings and General Praljak's challenges to the judgement in respect of his contribution as a commander of HVO armed forces. In his briefs in Grounds 40.2 and 40.7, Praljak claims errors in the Trial Chamber's findings that he contributed by using HVO armed forces to commit crimes. As with the evidence of his contribution as a conduit, the evidence of Praljak's contribution on the use of the HVO armed forces also tells us much about his criminal intent. Gornji Vakuf, Your Honours have heard a lot of about Gornji Vakuf today and in the previous days. At Gornji Vakuf, Praljak claims in Ground 42 that the events there were not planned and that he was not kept informed of the situation there. The Trial Chamber's findings to the contrary are reasonable. Your Honours, in my remarks over the next couple of minutes this will not only go to Praljak's challenges on his contribution in respect of the Gornji Vakuf operation and the crimes there, but this will also relate to our answer to Your Honours' question 4(c) to the extent it relates to Praljak's knowledge or the extent to which he was privy to the Siljeg report, Exhibit P1351. We know that after the ultimatum he was involved in drafting was issued, HVO Operative Zone Commander Siljeg and HVO Chief of Staff Miro Andric consulted with Praljak on the 16th of January about implementing it. By then Praljak had arrived from Mostar. He is referred to in Siljeg's report at 2000 hours on the 16th of January, that's P1162, as calling for the ABiH to accept the decisions of the HZ HB, that is, the ultimatum. Also on the 16th of January, Praljak issued orders for artillery such as rocket-launchers to be deployed in Gornji Vakuf. That's Exhibit P1172, referred to at volume 4, paragraph 558. Notably on the 23rd of January, the British Battalion peacekeepers in the area reported an HVO rocket attack at the village of Bistrica in Gornji Vakuf where the houses were burning fiercely. The report stressed: "This is most definitely ethnic cleansing by Croats on a Muslim village." That's Exhibit P1278. On the next day, the 24th of January, Petkovic ordered Siljeg to "report urgently to Brada." And Your Honours, Brada -- Praljak is referred to in some of the HVO's documentation as Brada, or Beard. "Report urgently to Brada in Mostar and send a report on the situation in Gornji Vakuf directly." That's P1293. Petkovic was in Geneva at the negotiations on the 24th at that time. Praljak was in charge and Siljeg was reporting to him on Petkovic's order. Other reports of Siljeg make clear that Praljak was well informed, was directing HVO operations and was even issuing orders to Siljeg himself. In P1277, the 23rd of January, Siljeg reports: "I issued necessary orders that were in the spirit of the orders issued by Brada and they were carried out." In his report on 26 January 1993, Siljeg again referred to the other orders of Brada that he carried out. P1311. See volume 4, paragraph 559 on that. The HVO's own documents thus confirm that Petkovic ordered Siljeg to report to Praljak regarding the Gornji Vakuf operation. Praljak was in direct, regular contact with Siljeg, and issued orders to him for HVO operations. The Trial Chamber thus reasonably found that Praljak planned, directed, facilitated, and was kept informed of ongoing events in Gornji Vakuf after the HVO launched its attacks there on the 18th of January. That finding is at volume 4, paragraphs 558 -- sorry, 558 to 562. Praljak knew about these HVO crimes, he intended them, he contributed to them. For the booths, I'm going to skip ahead in my outline to paragraph 64. Your Honours, this brings to us the second part of your question 4(c), where Your Honours invite us to address the significance of the Siljeg report and the extent to which Praljak may have been privy to its content. The series of HVO documents that I've just referred to clearly establishes that Praljak was privy to the information contained in Exhibit P1351, including HVO crimes. They show it was Praljak and Siljeg who were essentially co-directing the HVO military operations in Gornji Vakuf. Everything that Siljeg knew about the events in Gornji Vakuf, including the crimes referred to in Siljeg's report, were undoubtedly known to Praljak. Pursuant to Petkovic's order of 24 January, Siljeg was to report directly to Praljak, Brada, about Gornji Vakuf. There was no reason for Siljeg to withhold any information from Praljak contrary to Petkovic's order. We know that this report of Siljeg was sent to the Herceg-Bosna government, the Herceg-Bosna Defence Department, and the HVO Main Staff. And it reported the HVO crimes in Gornji Vakuf. Why would Siljeg have withheld that information from Praljak when it was reporting all of this information to the government, the Defence Department and to the Main Staff? Praljak knew the scale and the violent nature of the crimes directed against the Muslim population as referred to in Siljeg's report. Exhibit P1351. And, Your Honours, the Chamber should dismiss, therefore, Praljak's challenges to the Trial Chamber's findings on his contribution to the Gornji Vakuf crimes. And now for the booths, I'm going to skip ahead to paragraph 86 of my outline. I'm going to address, Your Honours, Praljak's contribution and awareness of the HVO crimes at Mostar, and in the course of doing that, I'll address your question number 8 and then I will conclude my remarks with a response to your question number 2 related to the Old Bridge. In regards to Mostar, Praljak claims he should be acquitted of any crimes that occurred prior to his taking command of the HVO Main Staff on the 24th of July, 1993, as well as any crimes after his departure and return to Croatia on the 9th of November, on the grounds that he was not involved in implementing the common criminal plan in Mostar during those periods. This is General Praljak's brief at paragraph 483. As to the post-November 9th period, Your Honours, Praljak has not been convicted of those crimes what occurred in Mostar or anywhere else after he quit the HVO on the 9th of November. In volume 4, paragraph 1228, the Trial Chamber found that he ceased being a member of the joint criminal enterprise at the time he left on the 9th of November. See our respondent's brief on that at paragraphs 177 and 179. So he's not responsible for what happened after the 9th of November. In terms of his responsibility for what happened prior to taking formal command of the HVO Main Staff on the 24th of July, we say that Praljak's misapplying the law of JCE when he claims he is not responsible for what happened in Mostar before the 24th of July. He was a member of the JCE from mid-January and he's therefore responsible for crimes committed by co-JCE members prior to the 24th of July, 1993, during the time that he was exercising de facto control rather than de jure control over the HVO armed forces. So, Your Honours, it's our position that he was properly convicted of all JCE 1 crimes committed in Mostar during the period of his JCE membership. Now, regarding Praljak's contribution to crimes committed in Mostar after the 24th of July, 1993, when he was commander of the HVO Main Staff and therefore exercising de jure authority and effective control over the HVO armed forces, Praljak claims that the Trial Chamber relied only on his functions as commander of the HVO Main Staff in finding that he contributed to the crimes. See his brief, paragraphs 428 and 431. He claims he didn't know about the crimes in Mostar, and that he did not possess the requisite mens rea. But before considering what he knew and how he contributed, let's first recall the situation in Mostar. And I'm going to do this briefly because I need to make sure to answer your questions 8 and 2. So the situation in East Mostar while Praljak was commander of the HVO Main Staff. The HVO shelled East Mostar "daily, intensely, and closely." That's volume 2, paragraph 1000. One international told the Trial Chamber that from September 1993, when Praljak was commander, East Mostar received on average between 20 to 100 HVO shelling impacts per day. That's volume 2, paragraph 1000. The densely populated Donja Mahala neighbourhood was hit not only by artillery and intense shelling, but also by improvised explosive devices in the form of tires filled with explosives that would be rolled into the town from HVO positions. Volume 2, paragraph 1005. The HVO conducted a test dropping two napalm bombs on Donja Mahala neighbourhood in August of 1993. It is referred to in a report directed to the HVO Main Staff, Praljak's Main Staff on the 17th of August. That's Exhibit 4265, volume 2, 1006. The Trial Chamber found that HVO sniping targeted women, children and elderly. People were targeted while carrying out daily activities like fetching water. Volume 2, paragraph 1185. What's more, when Praljak took command of the HVO Main Staff, waves of evictions of Muslims were happening already, well under way, from West Mostar across the Neretva River into East Mostar. This did not stop once Praljak took over. The campaign of violence, expulsion and appropriation of Muslim housing in West Mostar continued unabated. As I mentioned on Monday, during this period the number of Muslims living in besieged East Mostar, Your Honours, increased from 20.000 to 55.000 by late August 1993. Volume 2, paragraph 1200. The conditions were horrendous. So what was Praljak's role in all of this? The Trial Chamber reasonably concluded that Praljak played an important role in planning and directing the military operations in Mostar municipality during the time he was commander of the HVO Main Staff. Paragraph -- volume 4, paragraph 579. On assuming command of the HVO Main Staff, Praljak asserted firm control over the HVO armed forces. Within two weeks, his Main Staff took over command of what he called the defence of Mostar. That's Exhibit P3983. Praljak's order of 12 August 1993 mobilized all the manpower and materiel of the HVO armed forces to eliminate the Muslim terrorists from Mostar. Volume 4, paragraph 579. This order placed an HVO rocket and artillery regiment under the direct command of Praljak's Main Staff. Volume 1, paragraph 801. Thereafter, this artillery regiment sent reports to Praljak's Main Staff, including a report dated 25 August 1993 on its "intensive operations against targets in Mostar." That's P4495. On the 1st of September, Praljak issued an order on HVO military operations in Mostar, one objective of which was to clear Mostar of Muslim armed forces and in subsequent offensive operations to take control of Mostar. That's P4719. On the 24th of September, he issued a report to all Herceg-Bosna combatants entitled "Situation on the Mostar front," informing HVO armed forces of various developments, expressing his pride in their successful operations and exhorting them on to "new victories for the HRHB and all Croatian men and women. P5365, referred to at volume 4, paragraph 579. Your Honours, the level of Praljak's control and involvement in the HVO's Mostar operations confirms the Trial Chamber's finding that he participated in directing and planning HVO operations in Mostar as commander of the Main Staff. It is inconceivable that the substantial commitment of HVO assets, its men, its materiel to perpetuating the prolonged siege and attack on the Muslim population in East Mostar, including organised HVO operations to evict Muslims from West Mostar, targeting East Mostar with dozens or even hundreds of shells every day organised teams of snipers, it is inconceivable that this could have occurred for over three months, from the 24th of July to the 9th of November, 1993, without the knowledge and steadfast approval of the commander of the HVO Main Staff. Praljak's control and responsibility for the crimes in East Mostar was even confirmed by Croatia's leadership, specifically Defence Minister Susak when he was confronted with the HVO's crimes in East Mostar by US Ambassador Galbraith. On the 31st of August 1993, Galbraith spoke to Defence Minister Susak about reports of heavy shelling in East Mostar. He reported in the cable that he warned Susak of the potentially disastrous consequences should UN personnel be injured by HVO shelling. The cable states that: "Susak promised he would be immediately in touch with HVO Commander Praljak to demand a stop to the shelling." That's P9506. At trial, the Chamber asked Galbraith: "Were you certain that there was a link between Mr. Susak and Mr. Praljak and Mr. Praljak and the bombing?" And the answer was: "Yes." Croatia's conduit in Herceg-Bosnia had the authority to turn the HVO shelling on and off. The Chamber reasonably concluded that Praljak contributed to the HVO's crimes there and intended them. This brings me, Your Honours, to your question 8. You've asked us to consider whether the Trial Chamber made necessary findings on specific intent to spread terror and what the impact would be if the Trial Chamber were found not to have given a reasoned opinion on that. Our answer is that although the Trial Chamber did not explicitly say that Praljak possessed specific intent to spread terror, it did make the findings to that effect. As I'll explain in a little bit of more detail in a moment, the Trial Chamber correctly set out the law. It made, secondly, the underlying factual findings on terror. It found the HVO intended to spread terror, and it found Praljak intended the underlying components of the terror campaign. These findings make clear that in convicting Praljak of this crime, the Chamber concluded that he possessed specific intent to spread terror. First, on the law, the Trial Chamber addressed the elements of unlawful infliction of terror on civilians as charged in Count 25 in volume 4, paragraphs 195 to 197. It cited the appeals judgement in the Galic case when citing the elements. Second, throughout the judgement the Trial Chamber makes appropriate factual findings that the crime was committed. I referred to a number of these findings already in my submissions on Mostar and Praljak's contribution. The shelling, the siege, the sniping, the overcrowding, the conditions. In volume 3, paragraph 1689 to 1692, the Trial Chamber explicitly found that by intensely shelling and sniping at the Muslims of East Mostar, deliberately destroying the mosques as well as the Old Bridge, blocking humanitarian aid, targeting internationals, all the while keeping the civilians there in this increasingly overcrowded enclave, "the HVO primarily intended to spread terror among the civilian population of East Mostar." That's volume 3, paragraph 1692. And this is a point that was raised by His Honour Judge Meron yesterday, the finding that it was the HVO that intended terror, and I will return to this in a moment, Your Honour. If the HVO was anyone, it was Slobodan Praljak between the 24th of July and the 9th of the November, 1993. He contributed in multiple ways to those means that were used to spread terror in East Mostar. He intended the destruction of the structures and the mosques, the deliberate targeting of civilians, the murders, the woundings, physical and psychological abuse, and attacks on internationals. That's the Trial Chamber's finding at volume 4, paragraph 586. After making its underlying findings in volumes 2 and 3, the Trial Chamber expressly included unlawful infliction of terror as among the JCE 1 crimes in volume 4, paragraph 68. The Chamber expressly included the HVO's crimes against East Mostar in the crimes intended by Praljak. Volume 4, paragraphs 586, 625. Only after all of that did the Trial Chamber convict him of Count 25, in volume 4, paragraph 630. So yesterday, Your Honour, Judge Meron, you referred to the Galic appeals judgement and you drew the distinction between the intent of the accused versus the intent of a force. That's at transcript page 88. And indeed the Trial Chamber did find that the force, the HVO, intended terror. That's at volume 3, paragraph 1692. But it did not stop there. As I've just indicated, the Trial Chamber then went on to expressly include the crimes directed against East Mostar which form the basis of the overall terror finding and included those crimes in the crimes intended by Praljak. And it then went on to include those crimes in its finding of what was -- what were the crimes of -- the shared intent crimes of the JCE 1 and ultimately convicted Praljak of the crime of intent to spread terror. And so, Your Honours, we say that the only reasonable interpretation of all these findings is that the Trial Chamber was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that it was Praljak and not just the HVO who possessed specific intent to spread terror among the civilian population. And although the Trial Chamber could have made a more explicit finding on this point, there is no error or reason to invalidate Praljak's conviction. On this point, I refer Your Honours to the Martic appeal judgement, paragraph 181. In any event, if the Appeals Chamber finds there is insufficient reasoning in the judgement to uphold Praljak's Count 25 conviction, its own examination, your own examination, Your Honours, of the evidence and the underlying factual findings will lead to the same result of finding that Praljak intended to spread terror. In volume -- sorry, question 2, Your Honours, you have asked what would be the impact on the Trial Chamber's findings on persecution and infliction of terror as to Stojic and Praljak should it conclude that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that the destruction of the Old Bridge constituted wanton destruction as charged under Count 20? Our assumption, based on the parts of the Stojic and Praljak briefs that Your Honours have referred us to, is that Your Honours are inquiring what would be the impact if it were determined that the shelling attack on the Old Bridge was a proportionate, lawful attack; that is that the attack was justified by military necessity as opposed to the Trial Chamber's finding that it was a disproportionate attack. Were Your Honours to determine that the attack was justified by military necessity, there would be an impact on Stojic and Praljak's convictions for persecution and terror but it would be minimal. Before explaining why, I would like to preface my answer with an observation that forms the foundation of the Prosecution position on the relation between the crimes of wanton destruction, persecution, and intentional infliction of terror as applied to the attack on the Old Bridge. If the Old Bridge was targeted primarily to spread terror, if it was destroyed in order to contribute to the HVO's persecution campaign, then its destruction was not justified by military necessity. And this holds true whether or not the Old Bridge remained a military target on the date of its demise, the 9th of November, 1993. But on your question, a determination that the attack on the Old Bridge was proportionate and lawful would mean that the destruction of the Old Bridge could not form a part of the persecution and unlawful infliction of terror counts -- convictions, I should say. This is because the attack would not have been carried out with the primary intent to inflict terror or with the intent to discriminate. Since the findings on persecution and infliction of terror are based on an aggregation of numerous crimes and acts intended to discriminate against the Muslims or to inflict terror on those in Mostar, Stojic and Praljak's convictions for those crimes under Counts 1 and 25 would remain intact. On this, we refer Your Honours to the Trial Chamber's findings on the violations underpinning persecution, volume 3, paragraphs 1694 to 1741. And the findings such as shelling and sniping that comprise the overall finding on the crime of terror. Those are at volume 3, paragraphs 1689 to 1692. The destruction of the Old Bridge is just one feature of this, and so the persecution and terror convictions would stand even if the destruction of the Old Bridge is not a part of them. That said, Your Honours, we would offer these submissions on the unlawfulness of the destruction of the Old Bridge in response to the appellants' submissions. The attack implicates several different crimes as Your Honours know, wanton destruction, persecution, infliction of terror. All are distinct crimes with distinct elements, none of which can be considered in isolation. Above all, we stress that the attack must be considered in the context of the HVO's protracted campaign of persecution, shelling and sniping, that is, terror, directed against the Muslims of Mostar. We know that by November of 1993, the HVO and these appellants had for ten months been attacking, killing, imprisoning, violently expelling and deporting Muslims throughout Herceg-Bosna. This was ethnic cleansing on an extraordinary scale and it was on discriminatory grounds. We know that the conflict in Mostar began in early May 1993, and that from that point until the 9th of November, when the bridge collapsed into the Neretva River, the ABiH held a narrow slice of territory on the west bank of the Neretva River and during this period the Old Bridge was used as a supply line for both the ABiH and the large Muslim population, civilian population living in Donja Mahala on the west bank of the Neretva. So the Old Bridge was a lawful military target, but the totality of the evidence shows it was not targeted for that reason. We know that the repeated shelling attacks targeting the Old Bridge on the 8th of November rendered it completely unusable, that although it was still standing it could be considered destroyed. That's what the Trial Chamber found at volume 3, paragraphs 1300 and 1318. In other words, the bridge no longer had any military value. There was no military advantage to be gained by bringing about its complete obliteration and collapse into the river on the following day, the 9th. We know that the impetus for the final attack on the Old Bridge was not anything that had happened in Mostar. The impetus for this attack was the fall of Vares to the ABiH forces in distant Central Bosnia. The fall of Vares is expressly referred to by Petkovic in his 8 November 1993 attack order, P6534. The Trial Chamber reasonably concluded that the attack on Mostar on the 8th of November was a reaction to the fall of Vares. That's at volume 2, paragraph 1301. The European Community Monitors, the ECMM, in Bosnia, in Mostar, concluded the same thing on that very day. At volume 2, paragraph 1352, the Trial Chamber relied on an ECMM report of 9 November 1993. The ECMM assessment was: "The timing of the HVO action against the Old Bridge in Mostar could be linked to events in Vares and explained as a bloody-minded revenge. The consequences of its destruction should not be underestimated. It produced a feeling of despair in East Mostar, evidenced by the senior Muslim politicians literally reduced to tears. Evidence presented to ECMM convincingly demonstrates the targeting was deliberate and sustained. By choosing to destroy a monument to ethnic tolerance, the HVO have sent a strong but negative message to the Muslims." So, Your Honours, this attack was a payback, it was retribution. If the Old Bridge was targeted primarily to spread terror, if it was destroyed to contribute to the persecution campaign, its destruction was not justified by military necessity. IHL makes this clear. That an object may be a lawful target does not mean that IHL, international humanitarian law, will automatically authorise its destruction. Identifying a potentially lawful target is just the beginning of the inquiry. And the inquiry here leads to the conclusion that the ultimate destruction of the Old Bridge was not the result of a thoughtful, good faith application of the proportionality test. In his brief, Stojic refers to the literature telling us that a bridge is the archetypical military target. His brief paragraph 160. As though this bridge was no different --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Objection. Mr. President, I've remained seated on several occasions when my learned friend has used his opportunity to respond to General Petkovic's submissions by including the name and arguments of Mr. Bruno Stojic. Now, to raise arguments that are contained in our brief is to -- is to deny the appellant Mr. Stojic the right to respond, and I would ask that he be prevented from doing so. Your Honour, these arguments could have been raised yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's hear what Mr. Stringer has to say and then we'll decide. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think counsel's point is somewhat well taken. I think the better solution is to allow them to respond to us if the Chamber is so inclined. The Chamber's question number 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I would skip straight away to your next argument because I don't think what you did is the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so in considering the Trial Chamber's finding on the lawfulness of the destruction of the bridge, we submit, Your Honours, that the bridge was not destroyed because it was a military target, otherwise it would have been destroyed earlier, much earlier, in this lengthy campaign and siege. The cultural icon of the Old Bridge was destroyed in the latter stages of a lengthy and violent ethnic cleansing campaign. It was destroyed as retribution for events that had occurred in Vares, far removed from the Mostar battlefield. Its destruction was an attack directed against the Muslims of Mostar, not the ABiH. It was intended to spread terror and despair among the Muslim population who had been hanging on in Mostar since the siege started five months earlier, to extinguish any hope that their ordeal might end or their situation might improve. And so Your Honours' ruling affirming the unlawfulness of the destruction of the Old Bridge on the 9th of November would not undermine international law. It would not affect or -- it would not certainly be inconsistent with a finding that the destruction of the bridge was not lawful. It would, in fact, affirm that military commanders who do not apply principles of IHL in good faith, those whose targeting decisions are demonstrably intended to terrorise and persecute civilians based on ethnicity will find no protection in the law of armed conflict. Now, if Your Honours have any -- no more questions on this or any of my submissions, I'm ready to pass the floor to my colleague, Ms. Finnin. Let me make one correction. Line 75 -- transcript page 75, line 23 should read "volume 1," paragraphs 195 to 197, not "volume 4."

utterances.speaker: MS. FINNIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Sarah Finnin and I will be addressing questions 6 and 7 which relate to Stupni Do and conditions of confinement at Dretelj and Gabela. For the remainder of Praljak's arguments concerning Vares and his role in detention centres, we rely on our written response to Grounds 32, 45, 46, and 54. In question 6, Your Honours have asked us to address whether the evidence establishes that Praljak knew UNPROFOR was seeking access to Stupni Do between 23 and 25 October 1993 and that he sought to prevent such access. Your Honours have asked us to focus in particular on Exhibits P6068 and P6073.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FINNIN
utterances.text: I intend to give Your Honours a short outline of our answer and then I'll address each of our points in more detail. Our answer to Your Honours' question is yes. The HVO's own communications as well as UNPROFOR and ECMM reports establish that in the days immediately following the attack on Stupni Do, Praljak and others within the HVO Main Staff were aware of allegations of a massacre. Instead of taking swift action against the perpetrators, they facilitated efforts to keep UNPROFOR out of the village for as long as possible, buying time while the HVO attempted to cover up their crimes. The two exhibits Your Honours have referred to in the question tell part of this story. In the next few minutes I will put those exhibits in the context of what was occurring at the time, both on the ground and within the HVO Main Staff. The Chamber found that HVO special units under the command of Ivica Rajic attacked the Muslim village of Stupni Do on the morning of Saturday, 23 October 1993. During the attack, HVO soldiers murdered 28 civilians, including women, elderly, and children as young as 2. Some were shot at close range. Others had their throats cut. Many were burned alive in their homes. Volume 3, paragraphs 410 to 467. UNPROFOR became aware of the attack on Saturday afternoon when patrols in the area sighted smoke and heard firing coming from the direction of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a question, please. What was the date on the Saturday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MS. FINNIN
utterances.text: That was 23 October 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FINNIN
utterances.text: UNPROFOR became aware of the attack on the Saturday, 23 October. That's P7838, page 2, and P10202, pages 1 to 2. They immediately made attempts to reach the village. For three days these attempts were consistently blocked by HVO soldiers who set up roadblocks, mined check-points around the village, and fired on UNPROFOR vehicles. P7838, page 2. For those three days, the village continued to burn. P6098, and P10202, pages 1 and 8. In the view of UNPROFOR's force commander, it was clear that the HVO troops were "attempting to hide from us the atrocities they had committed." P6182. But under unrelenting pressure from UNPROFOR and in the face of widespread allegations of a massacre the HVO finally broke. On Monday, 25 October, UN Military Observer Patrick Martin managed to convince Commander Rajic to escort him through Stupni Do. P7838, and P10202, pages 7 to 10. Then believing there was nothing implicating them in a massacre, the HVO at last gave UNPROFOR full access to the village. So on Tuesday, 26 October, UNPROFOR's Nordic Battalion was allowed in, along with other internationals and members of the press. P7838. Despite the HVO's attempts to tamper with the scene, enough evidence remained for UNPROFOR to confirm that a massacre had occurred. P6182, and P10084, paragraphs 19 to 22. The Trial Chamber reasonably concluded that Praljak was specifically informed of murders and destruction of property occurring in Stupni Do no later than 5 November 1993. That's volume 4, paragraph 595. This was the day he attended a meeting with Tudjman and other key JCE members where the events of Stupni Do were discussed at length. P6454. However, the Chamber also recognised that Praljak was aware of allegations of crimes well before this meeting, when UNPROFOR was seeking access to the village. That's volume 4, paragraph 621. This finding is well supported by the evidence. The evidence establishes that Praljak began receiving reports about what had happened in Stupni Do on the very same day as the attack. That Saturday evening, Rajic sent a one-page report to Petkovic. P6026. Praljak admitted to receiving this report at around 11.00 that same night, 23 October. Transcript page 41900. In this report, Rajic states that in the morning hours he carried out an attack on Stupni Do and that "some civilians were killed." In the days to follow, reports of a massacre began to spread. On Sunday, 24 October, international representatives on the ground are reporting to their superiors about a suspected massacre at Stupni Do. For example, P6055. UNPROFOR's Nordic Battalion has already been tasked with getting into the village to search for signs of a massacre. P6053, page 3. And UNPROFOR Command has already informed the HVO's liaison officer of their concerns and has sent a letter of protest to Boban and Petkovic. P6053, page 3. The HVO Main Staff - Praljak's HVO Main Staff - immediately goes into damage control. Their liaison officer to the UN tries to placate UNPROFOR, dismissing claims of a massacre as doubtful. P6049. But by Monday, 25 October, the HVO has lost control of the story. Croatian TV is claiming to have footage of the massacre, and the Main Staff in Citluk is scrambling to come up with a position. That's P6104 and P6091. By now, Rajic has escorted Patrick Martin through Stupni Do and believes there are no bodies to be found as "the area has been cleaned up." P6102. Armed with Rajic's assurances that no footage of the massacre exists, the Main Staff issues an announcement denying the allegations. P6102 and P6083. Late that evening, that's 25 October, Petkovic is summoned to UNPROFOR to discuss access to Stupni Do. P6144, and P6454, page 59. It's at this point that the HVO finally buckles under the pressure. Petkovic writes to Rajic urgently, ordering him to "allow the UN to enter Stupni Do tomorrow, whatever the consequences (understand that the more difficult it is made for them, the worse it is for us)." P6078, and also P6454, pages 59 to 60, and P6144. The following day UNPROFOR is given full access to the village. The evidence shows that during this critical period, Praljak and the HVO Main Staff facilitated Rajic's efforts to keep UNPROFOR out of Stupni Do. I'll now take Your Honours to two examples which illustrate this. The first example is a series of orders or reports coming from within the HVO Main Staff on 24 and 25 October. And this includes the exhibits referred to in Your Honours' question. At 5.00 p.m. on Sunday evening, that's the 24th, as UNPROFOR is continuing to seek access to Stupni Do, Rajic submits a report about UNPROFOR directly to Praljak himself. This is P6067. Rajic asks Praljak to please warn UNPROFOR to withdraw. And he states: "If not, we shall be forced to intervene and we cannot be held responsible for the consequences." As I said, Rajic's report was addressed to Praljak. Within just hours, Rajic receives a reply. P6066. That reply comes from Tole, Praljak's Chief of Staff. It orders that anti-armour weaponry be positioned around UNPROFOR and that UNPROFOR be warned that they will be destroyed if they interfere with the HVO's combat activities. Through this order the Main Staff has effectively authorised the use of force against UNPROFOR. It is inconceivable that Tole, Praljak's Chief of Staff, would do this without Praljak's approval, that he would direct the HVO to essentially blockade UNPROFOR and potentially engage them in combat. That evening, UNPROFOR forces are fired upon by the HVO. Transcript page 24437 to 24438, and Exhibit P2980, pages 15 to 16. This brings me to the exhibits referred to in Your Honours' question. In Exhibit P6073, Petkovic informs Praljak that "in Vares our men fired at the UN and drove them away. I'm trying to rectify the situation." And, Your Honours, this is coming after the HVO has fired on UNPROFOR the previous evening. Praljak responds in Exhibit P6068 by ordering Petkovic to disguise the HVO's attempts to keep UNPROFOR out of Stupni Do. He states: "Do whatever it takes to give the impression that we did not drive the UN away from Vares by opening fire." That's also at transcript page 24572. This interaction confirms both that Praljak knew Rajic was preventing UNPROFOR from uncovering the HVO's crimes and that Praljak supported it. Turning now to the second example. This is Praljak's order issued on the evening of Saturday, 23 October. As I mentioned earlier, at 11.00 p.m. on Saturday, 23 October, Praljak received a report from Rajic stating that he had carried out an attack on Stupni Do and that some civilians were killed. The report also indicated that three local HVO officials had been placed in isolation because "they attempted to obstruct the planned activities." P6026. It is on the bottom of this report that Praljak handwrites his order to "sort out the situation in Vares, showing no mercy towards anyone." P6026 and P6028. In his appeal brief, Praljak has spoken at great length about this order and what it means. He claims, for example, that it isn't really an order and he claims it wasn't intended to be distributed among HVO soldiers. But it is order. It is an order coming from the commander of the HVO Main Staff and it's treated that way. It is typed and distributed by packet communication to a number of Praljak's subordinates in Central Bosnia, including Rajic himself. That's P6028. Praljak also claims in his brief that the Chamber misinterpreted his words. He claims this instruction to sort out the situation was concerned with internal problems and local quarrels within the HVO and was issued in response to reports of smuggling. And he denies the order had anything to do with the crimes committed in Stupni Do. Even taking Praljak at his word, this misses the point. In this order, Praljak does not even acknowledge Rajic's report that civilians were killed during the attack on Stupni Do. He shows no concern whatsoever for the possibility that his subordinates have committed crimes. Instead, through this order he effectively gives his subordinates, including Rajic, the very commander responsible for the attack, he effectively gives them carte blanche to act however they see fit. And he also gives Rajic all the authority that he needs to cover up the HVO's crimes. And Rajic did exactly that, giving direct orders to severely restrict movement around Vares municipality while his forces attempted to clean up Stupni Do. P6114, P6126, and P10080, pages 221 to 228. Even when more and more alarming information emerges about a potential massacre, Praljak still doesn't act to hold Rajic to account or even to curb his crimes. Instead, he facilitates Rajic's efforts to conceal those crimes by keeping UNPROFOR out, as we see in the interaction occurring over the next two days. On the basis of this evidence, Your Honours should uphold the Chamber's reasonable conclusion that Praljak sought to prevent UNPROFOR from accessing Stupni Do and uncovering the consequences of the HVO's crimes. Unless Your Honours have any questions concerning Stupni Do, I'll now move to question 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FINNIN
utterances.text: Before addressing Your Honours question, question 7, we would first note that by virtue of Praljak's shared intent and his significant contribution to the JCE, Praljak is criminally responsible for all JCE 1 crimes committed in the HVO's network of detention facilities, not just the crimes he was personally aware of and not just the crimes he personally contributed to. That's Sainovic appeals judgement, paragraph 1491; and Karemera appeals judgement, paragraphs 109 and 153. As such, Praljak's awareness of conditions of confinement in Dretelj and Gabela does not impact his criminal responsibility for crimes committed in those facilitates or in any of the other HVO detention facilities. In terms of his JCE 1 liability, his awareness of the conditions in those two prisons only bears on the question of his failure to make any real effort to improve the conditions there, this being part of his significant contribution to the JCE. So to return to Your Honours' question, our answer is that Praljak was aware that the conditions of confinement in those prisons were so serious as to amount to crimes and he knew this by September 1993 at the latest, when publication of images of emaciated detainees sparked international outrage. Given this knowledge, his failure to make any real effort to improve those conditions properly formed part of his significant contribution to the JCE. Again, I'll give Your Honours an outline of our argument and then I'll address each of our points in more detail. The Trial Chamber took a conservative approach in its analysis of Praljak's awareness of crimes committed in Dretelj and Gabela. It concluded that from September 1993, Praljak was aware that the conditions in Gabela were problematic enough to bring about Tudjman's intervention, and that the conditions in Dretelj were poor. That's volume 4, paragraphs 609, 611, 614. However, the evidence establishes much more than that. In light of the information that was available to Praljak once he took control of the HVO Main Staff on 24 July 1993, it is simply implausible that he was not aware of the deplorable nature of the conditions to which Dretelj and Gabela detainees were subjected. Even before taking up that position, Praljak was already playing a crucial role as the link between Croatian officials and members of the HVO, a role that required that he remain informed of developments on the ground in Herceg-Bosna and that he keep Croatia informed of those developments. As a result, the only reasonable conclusion was that Praljak was aware, just as Tudjman was, that the conditions in those prisons were so serious as to amount to crimes. And yet despite having the power to put a stop to those crimes, Praljak allowed them to continue. It was only in the face of an international scandal which forced Tudjman himself to intervene, it was only then that Praljak did anything. And even then, he made no real effort to remedy the conditions. In the end, nothing really changed. I'll spend the next few minutes taking Your Honours through each of these points in more detail. Beginning with Praljak's knowledge of the conditions in Dretelj and Gabela. I'll take Your Honours through some of the information that was available to Praljak during the relevant period, information that was either in the public domain or information that was otherwise available to him. But before I do that, I'll just spend a moment setting out the situation regarding the camps at the time Praljak took over as HVO commander on 24 July. Your Honours will recall that on 30 June 1993 Petkovic issued an order which resulted in a massive campaign to arrest and detain Muslim men. Volume 4, paragraphs 57 and 890. By the time Praljak took over as commander of the HVO Main Staff on 24 July, several thousand Muslim detainees were already unlawfully detained in both Dretelj and Gabela. By that time, that's 24 July, the conditions in which those detainees were being held were already so serious as to constitute inhumane acts and inhumane treatment. As Galbraith testified, by that time, 24 July, the US had been putting pressure on Croatia to put a stop to HVO crimes, including inhumane conditions of detention for over a month. That's transcript pages 6424 to 6425, 6477 to 6480, 6505, and 6541. Also by that time, 24 July, while international representatives had not yet been permitted access to Dretelj and Gabela, there was growing concern about the treatment of detainees. For example, transcript pages 17255, 17265, 17267 to 17268, and Exhibits P3271, P3952, and P4863. That was the situation Praljak faced when he took over from Petkovic as commander of the HVO Main Staff. In just over a month, conditions at Dretelj and Gabela became world news. By the end of August, there was graphic evidence of the appalling conditions at Dretelj, graphic evidence which was immediately reported on by the press. Praljak claims in his brief that he wasn't aware of this press coverage at the time. Before addressing Praljak's claim, let me just take Your Honours to what was being reported and where. The reports on conditions in the camps initially came from a group of Muslim detainees who were released in late August and forced to cross the front line into ABiH-held territory in Jablanica. That's 2D411, page 3; P977B; and transcript page 17266. Your Honours, if we could go into private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FINNIN
utterances.text: Thank you. As described in Exhibit 4D801, page 3, the shocking images of those detainees "went around the world, just like those of the Omarska camp inmates a year before." For example, footage of those detainees appeared on both French TV 5 and also on Croatian TV. Your Honours, in just a moment we will play that footage for you. It takes about a minute. It's Exhibit P977A, identified at trial by Malovic at transcript pages 14342 to 14344, and 14346.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I remind you that you have just under ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. FINNIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "These people just arrived to Jablanica. A bit earlier during their release, their Croat captors amused themselves by forcing them to run under rifle fire. Four people got killed on that occasion. Their skinny bodies bear witness to a horrible treatment they underwent and their statements reveal bestialities. Packed in warehouses, starved, unbearably thirsty. In order to survive they had to drink their own urine. "Detention in the Dretelj and Gabela camps confirms again the daily horror that reigns in detention camps in Bosnia. According to the testimonies collected by the UNHCR, they were constantly beaten and burned with cigarettes. Some of them died immediately. Croatian soldiers amused themselves by opening fire from automatic rifles on warehouses where they were kept. Thirty of them got wounded in that way. In addition to physical, there was also mental torture. They had to sing the songs that were derogatory for Muslims. UNHCR employees claim that those people are nowadays desperate and humiliated. In the Dretelj camp, there are allegedly two to two and a half thousand detainees."

utterances.speaker: MS. FINNIN
utterances.text: The transcript of that video is attached to Exhibit P977A. An interview with UNHCR spokesperson Ray Wilkinson was also broadcast on CNN and Croatian TV. That's Exhibit P977B, identified at transcript pages 14471 to 14474. In that footage, Wilkinson described what these former Dretelj detainees were telling UNHCR about the conditions and he expressed UNHCR's concern that the conditions were deteriorating rapidly. Praljak denied seeing or even being told that this footage existed, footage that appeared on Croatian TV. He claimed at trial, for example: "I wasn't watching television during those days, nor did I have the time or possibility to do so." Transcript page 44328. Praljak's claim that he was unaware of the seriousness of the situation and the attention it was getting in the international press is simply not worthy of belief. Particularly in light of the evidence that Praljak was taking a very active interest in the way the media was reporting on the conflict. This is revealed, for example, by his angry complaints to ECMM in late September that: "He was not prepared to see more stories claiming that the Muslims are the victims." P5356, pages 2 to 3. In any event, Praljak admitted that in light of the international scandal, Tudjman himself was forced to react. Transcript page 44332. By 6 September, that's one week after the story of the Dretelj detainees broke, US ambassador Galbraith had met with Croatia's Foreign Minister Granic. P9057. Galbraith urged "in the strongest possible terms" that Zagreb demand the Bosnian Croats grant immediate access to detainees. That same day, 6 September, Tudjman sent a formal letter to Mate Boban calling on him to ensure international humanitarian law regarding the treatment of prisoners was strictly observed. P9497, pages 5 to 6, and also Galbraith, transcript pages 6505 to 6509, and Exhibit P9508. It's in the midst of all this that Praljak was allowing members of the press into the prisons, when images of emaciated Dretelj detainees were already appearing in the news, when Tudjman and other senior Croatian officials were being put under increasing pressure by the US to take action, and when the ICRC was finally being allowed entry into Dretelj and Gabela. This is when Praljak began to take action. Information about the conditions continued to emerge throughout September. And on 14 September, even the UN Security Council was expressing "its profound concern over recent reports that Bosnian Croats have been holding Bosnian Muslims in detention camps under deplorable conditions." P5047. By 24 September, Praljak himself was forced to admit during a meeting with ECMM that Dretelj was "a bad thing." P5356. In light of this evidence, Your Honours, the only reasonable conclusion was that Praljak was aware that the conditions in Dretelj and Gabela constituted crimes by September 1993 at the latest. In fact, it was his job to know. Praljak was not only commander of the HVO Main Staff. He was also the link between Croatia's senior leadership and the HVO. As Mr. Stringer has already outlined, it was his job to provide advice to Croatia's leadership regarding the military and political situation in BiH and to implement Croatia's policies on BiH territory through his authority over the HVO. So once the international pressure regarding the conditions of confinement in HVO detention facilities became so great that Tudjman himself was forced to do something, it was Praljak who stepped in and gave the impression that something was being done. When in reality very little changed for the detainees in those prisons. The Chamber carefully examined Praljak's claims to have taken steps to improve conditions and it reasonably concluded that these measures did not constitute a real effort to remedy the situation. This conclusion is supported by the Chamber's factual findings that crimes continued in Dretelj until it closed in early October 1993. And rather than being released, many Dretelj detainees were transferred to other HVO facilities including Gabela. There the crimes continued into December 1993. In these circumstances, the Chamber was correct to treat Praljak's failure to remedy the conditions in those military prisons as part of his contribution to the JCE. Unless Your Honours have any questions, that completes our response to Praljak's appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No questions. You have three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. FINNIN
utterances.text: That completes our submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Pinter, your client took ten minutes. You had still about five, six minutes left. So you have 25, 26 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have reorganised myself during the break and I believe I will succeed in saying all that I wished. First of all, I would like to follow up on my presentation on appeal and then I would proceed to respond to the Prosecution. The Defence of Slobodan Praljak wishes to draw the attention of the Appeals Chamber, that in assessing the grounds of appeal and the determinations, the findings of the Trial Chamber in their verdict, should bear in mind that the charges against Slobodan Praljak refer to the time of the fiercest offensive in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that findings should be made based on the actual state of facts and context of the time not in the general vision of an armed conflict between two armies, which would be impossible. The Defence also wishes to draw your attention to the fact that it's necessary to assess the incidents and events in the context in which they belong, that is to say, regarding Slobodan Praljak, to the extent that he was able to present the context and as we see it from the case file, the testimony of witnesses and all our submissions. The grounds of our appeal and the underlying arguments which we adhere to in full point out to such a number of errors in law and in fact made by the Trial Chamber, that is to say, the majority of the Trial Chamber, and thereby negation of law and especially violations of due process that even you cannot remedy. The Trial Chamber should have enabled the equality of arms to the parties in the presentation of evidence. They should not have given advantage to any of the sides in the presentation of evidence, according to Article 2.4 of the Statute. The points in our appeal to the effect that Slobodan Praljak was deprived of a fair trial because the presumption of innocence principle was violated as well as the principle of equality of arms and the premises of fair trial, there were also violations of Article 23.2 of the Statute described in grounds of appeal 5, 10.1, 37.2, 49, 50.1, paragraphs 558, and Ground 55.1 and 53. Without any statement of reasons given by the Trial Chamber, Slobodan Praljak was also deprived of his right to appeal. Equality of arms was described in Grounds 39.1, 52, 51, and 53, as well as 10.1, because the procedural rights of Slobodan Praljak and those of the Prosecution were not balanced, and we are right in saying that Slobodan Praljak did not have the right to a fair trial. In addition to that, the facts were not determined properly and a reduction of facts also leads to a negation of justice. Da mihi factum, dabo tibi ius is still a valid legal principle. Failure to apply the standard beyond a reasonable doubt is described in grounds of appeal 4, 9, 10.1, 12, 15, 20, 23, 38.2, 39.3, 41.3, 42, and 44.1. The Trial Chamber also failed to apply the standard in dubio pro reo that we referred to in our ground of appeal 38. With regard to the ground of appeal 50, in connection with the introduction of Ratko Mladic's diaries, we elaborated it in paragraphs 539 to 565 of our appeal brief. With the improper procedure described with all the references to findings and Defence submissions and the admission into evidence of the written statement ground of appeal 50.1, paragraphs 547 and 548, the majority made a decision with the intent of Slobodan Praljak regarding the joint criminal enterprise and joint criminal purpose without giving Slobodan Praljak the possibility to confront the said evidence, to provide explanations and to respond. More detail is given in paragraph 564 of Ground 50.2.
