We heard more today about Mladic's diaries and the evidence they are supposed to provide in a deformed procedure, we submit, we led to violations of Defence rights and the right to a fair trial. In our ground of appeal 51, the Defence points out that the Trial Chamber, that is to say, the majority, resorted to reducing some facts, simplifying them, which simplification necessarily leads to errors in findings and determination of key facts by rejecting a considerable number of Defence evidence. I am referring especially to the dissenting opinion of the Presiding Judge of the 16th of February, 2010, which dissenting opinion explains why he does not agree with the majority. The groundless simplification and reduction of facts that were to be assessed meant, as far as Slobodan Praljak is concerned, a conviction with regard to the existence of the JCE, de facto control, effective control, and at the same time there was a failure to apply the in dubio pro reo principles. By decision of the Trial Chamber, that is to say, the majority, most of the decisions regarding Slobodan Praljak were made by the majority, Defence evidence was rejected, evidence that was in response and in rebuttal of Prosecution evidence. Slobodan Praljak did not receive certification to appeal, and the Trial Chamber applied a double standard to the Prosecution and to the Defence. Concerning relevance, other failures to admit Defence evidence is referred to in paragraphs 567 to 576 of our appeal brief. It is impossible to respond to all the charges in the indictment if the Defence is not given the opportunity to present the events and the reasons why certain incidents happened. The Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna did not exist in a vacuum. General Praljak did not operate in a vacuum. Before making a verdict, the Trial Chamber needs to have at its disposal all the available facts in order to arrive at a just verdict. Events cannot be taken out of context. It is impossible to judge the mens rea of General Praljak without determining the pattern of conduct. His motivations, his actions. And if all of this together is not linked into a causal nexus, it is impossible to make a finding on criminal intent without hearing evidence that explain the reasons for the conduct of the president of the Republic of Croatia, the HVO, and General Praljak. It is not in doubt that the crimes charged in the indictment have been committed. However, in order to conflict General Praljak of these crimes, it is necessary to make a comprehensive presentation of events, not a partial one. It is necessary to assess the conduct of the international community. What were the actions of the important international players and what they said about the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I wish to draw your attention also to the allegations in the 51st ground of Prosecution's appeal pursuant to Rule 92 bis evidence and especially the statements regarding the Mujahedin in Central Bosnia and the situation in Central Bosnia. Such evidence and statements were rejected as irrelevant. In footnote 1298 of the appeal brief, there are numbers of statements that were rejected, especially the statement of Ali Ahmad Ali Hamad [phoen] and the transcript of his evidence in case IT-04-83-T. The position of the majority that witness statements referring to the Mujahedin and the events in Central Bosnia, Travnik, Bugojno, Kakanj were not relevant to the present case was erroneous because it was precisely the Prosecution that claimed in its indictment that one of the ways of conducting, carrying out the JCE was the unjustified terrorising and intimidation of Croats, telling them that they are threatened by the Mujahedin in order to achieve reverse expulsion and transfer of Croats from Central Bosnia to Herzegovina. The stand of the majority regarding these statements, namely that they were irrelevant, was certainly erroneous and, as such, enabled the finding from paragraphs 54 and 55 of volume 4 that HVO and Slobodan Praljak conceived a transfer of Croats and the threat from the Mujahedin in the absence of any real danger. Furthermore, I would like to emphasise our ground of appeal 53 just to show the bias of the Trial Chamber regarding the Defence of General Praljak. The Chamber rejected the expert report of Professor Sakic, paragraph 377, volume 1, and concluded that the report was not credible because it originates from the Ivo Pilar Institute which is associated with the Croatian government and Croatian Intelligence Services, which casts doubt on the impartiality of expert Sakic. However, neither the Republic of Croatia nor its intelligence services were parties to the case. At the same time when expert Sakic was rejected as an expert because of his association with Croatia, Witness Tomljanovich was presenting his report which was admitted by the Chamber and it served as a basis for the judgement. The Defence of General Praljak finds this conclusion of the Chamber as partial against Slobodan Praljak and judges such a finding as a confirmation that his basic right to a fair trial and the standard of presumption of innocence were violated. In his reply to the appeal, the Prosecution emphasises that the appeal of General Praljak is repetitive, that we repeat arguments and facts made during the trial and which were rejected at the time. It is true that we are reiterating arguments even now, not only in our appeal brief, we are repeating them in our submissions because they need to be heard and read, and most importantly, Slobodan Praljak, in view of his general right of the accused to receive clear and precise reasoning as to which acts or omissions justify the rejection of his arguments and evidence, what he should have done differently, more or better than he had done, in order to receive a verdict that gives a proper answer to his questions so that he may understand why he was convicted [as interpreted]. The errors of the Trial Chamber emphasised in our appeal brief were made against the rights of Slobodan Praljak. The Appeals Chamber cannot remedy them. It would be contrary to the generally accepted standards in the appeal procedure to try to remedy them now. The violations were made during the criminal procedure, and we should remain in that procedure. So we stand by our submission that Slobodan Praljak should be acquitted on all charges and that the judgement, due to all the errors made, should be invalidated and a re-trial be reordered. That would be all our submissions for now, but if we have any time left, I would like to proceed to respond to the Prosecution's reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I please be heard very briefly. We have just heard at least 20 minutes of Praljak appeal, which should have been a part of the appeals submissions. I'm going to be asking Your Honours to give us those three minutes, back, if I may.

As regards the other answers to your questions, perhaps my learned friend Mr. Stringer can reply first and then I might make use of a minute or two I have left.

utterances.text: I'm giving Mr. Stringer three minutes. Because rather than replying to his submissions, you raised new issues. I was expecting that because we gave you the floor during the reply time. So, however, we have to rectify that. Mr. Stringer, you have three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Grateful for your willingness to be flexible. Just a few words in response to the submissions on the Mladic diary entries. The Trial Chamber, after granting the Prosecution motion to re-open its case, the Mladic diaries came in at the very latter part of the case, granted the Prosecution -- allowed the two excerpts that Your Honours have seen in these proceedings. The Chamber then invited the Defence to file motions to re-open in order to respond to those which had been admitted. Slobodan Praljak tendered 24 exhibits, 22 of which were found by the Trial Chamber not to have any bearing on the diary entries or really much relevance to the case at all. He tendered also an expert -- well, a report of a handwriting expert but he tendered it under Rule 89, ICTY Rule 89 as opposed to 94 bis on experts, and the Trial Chamber very correctly ruled -- excluded the expert report. Praljak never indicated to the Chamber what it was he would say. He never made a submission that would justify re-opening his case, and the Trial Chamber had no basis on which to really make a decision as to whether the standards for re-opening had been met or would be met by whatever it was that Slobodan Praljak wanted to say because he never gave the Trial Chamber any indication whatsoever. It did note, however, that his desire to actually tender some of the Mladic diaries indicated that it was inconsistent with his challenges to the diaries on the other hand. Finally the Chamber offered and allowed him the opportunity to brief and make submissions on the diaries in closing submissions, and then at the closing submissions themselves, Defence counsel told the Chamber that he did not wish to expand, in closing argument, on the submissions made in the final trial brief about the Mladic diaries. So Praljak didn't give the Chamber a sufficient basis in which to re-open. He was granted nonetheless the opportunity to address this in closing, both written and orally. And then last point, Your Honour, as we've heard, Banovina, division of Bosnia, those points that are referred to in the Mladic diary entries are found throughout lots of other evidence in this case and they don't have an impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
